q: Which term matches this definition? “nonstriated, mononucleated muscle in the skin that is associated with hair follicles; assists in moving materials in the walls of internal organs, blood vessels, and internal passageways”
why: smooth muscle: nonstriated, mononucleated muscle in the skin that is associated with hair follicles; assists in moving materials in the walls of internal organs, blood vessels, and internal passageways

card.q: Why is elasticity an important quality of muscle tissue?
card.a: It allows muscle to return to its original length during relaxation after contraction.

q: The correct order for the smallest to the largest unit of organization in muscle tissue is ________.
why: The correct answer is: filament, myofibril, muscle fiber, fascicle. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Depolarization of the sarcolemma means ________.
options: the inside of the membrane has become less negative as sodium ions accumulate
the outside of the membrane has become less negative as sodium ions accumulate
the inside of the membrane has become more negative as sodium ions accumulate
the sarcolemma has completely lost any electrical charge
why: The correct answer is: the inside of the membrane has become less negative as sodium ions accumulate. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “neurotransmitter that binds at a motor end-plate to trigger depolarization”
why: acetylcholine (ACh): neurotransmitter that binds at a motor end-plate to trigger depolarization

q: Which term matches this definition? “protein that makes up most of the thin myofilaments in a sarcomere muscle fiber”
why: actin: protein that makes up most of the thin myofilaments in a sarcomere muscle fiber

q: Which term matches this definition? “change in voltage of a cell membrane in response to a stimulus that results in transmission of an electrical signal; unique to neurons and muscle fibers”
why: action potential: change in voltage of a cell membrane in response to a stimulus that results in transmission of an electrical signal; unique to neurons and muscle fibers

q: Which term matches this definition? “broad, tendon-like sheet of connective tissue that attaches a skeletal muscle to another skeletal muscle or to a bone”
why: aponeurosis: broad, tendon-like sheet of connective tissue that attaches a skeletal muscle to another skeletal muscle or to a bone

q: Which term matches this definition? “to reduce the voltage difference between the inside and outside of a cell’s plasma membrane (the sarcolemma for a muscle fiber), making the inside less negative than at rest”
why: depolarize: to reduce the voltage difference between the inside and outside of a cell’s plasma membrane (the sarcolemma for a muscle fiber), making the inside less negative than at rest

q: Which term matches this definition? “loose, and well-hydrated connective tissue covering each muscle fiber in a skeletal muscle”
why: endomysium: loose, and well-hydrated connective tissue covering each muscle fiber in a skeletal muscle

card.q: Watch this video to learn more about macro- and microstructures of skeletal muscles. (a) What are the names of the “junction points” between sarcomeres? (b) What are the names of the “subunits” within the myofibrils that run the length of skeletal muscle fibers? (c) What is the “double strand of pearls” described in the video? (d) What gives a skeletal muscle fiber its striated appearance?
card.a: (a) Z-lines. (b) Sarcomeres. (c) This is the arrangement of the actin and myosin filaments in a sarcomere. (d) The alternating strands of actin and myosin filaments.

card.q: Every skeletal muscle fiber is supplied by a motor neuron at the NMJ. Watch this video to learn more about what happens at the neuromuscular junction. (a) What is the definition of a motor unit? (b) What is the structural and functional difference between a large motor unit and a small motor unit? Can you give an example of each? (c) Why is the neurotransmitter acetylcholine degraded after binding to its receptor?
card.a: (a) It is the number of skeletal muscle fibers supplied by a single motor neuron. (b) A large motor unit has one neuron supplying many skeletal muscle fibers for gross movements, like the Temporalis muscle, where 1000 fibers are supplied by one neuron. A small motor has one neuron supplying few skeletal muscle fibers for very fine movements, like the extraocular eye muscles, where six fibers are supplied by one neuron. (c) To avoid prolongation of muscle contraction.

card.q: What would happen to skeletal muscle if the epimysium were destroyed?
card.a: Muscles would lose their integrity during powerful movements, resulting in muscle damage.

card.q: Describe how tendons facilitate body movement.
card.a: When a muscle contracts, the force of movement is transmitted through the tendon, which pulls on the bone to produce skeletal movement.

card.q: What are the five primary functions of skeletal muscle?
card.a: Produce movement of the skeleton, maintain posture and body position, support soft tissues, encircle openings of the digestive, urinary, and other tracts, and maintain body temperature.

card.q: What are the opposite roles of voltage-gated sodium channels and voltage-gated potassium channels?
card.a: The opening of voltage-gated sodium channels, followed by the influx of Na⁺, transmits an Action Potential after the membrane has sufficiently depolarized. The delayed opening of potassium channels allows K⁺ to exit the cell, to repolarize the membrane.

q: In relaxed muscle, the myosin-binding site on actin is blocked by ________.
why: The correct answer is: tropomyosin. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: According to the sliding filament model, binding sites on actin open when ________.
why: The correct answer is: calcium ion levels rise. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The cell membrane of a muscle fiber is called ________.
why: The correct answer is: sarcolemma. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Muscle relaxation occurs when ________.
options: calcium ions are actively transported out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
calcium ions diffuse out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
calcium ions are actively transported into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
calcium ions diffuse into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
why: The correct answer is: calcium ions are actively transported into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: During muscle contraction, the cross-bridge detaches when ________.
options: the myosin head binds to an ADP molecule
the myosin head binds to an ATP molecule
why: The correct answer is: the myosin head binds to an ATP molecule. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Thin and thick filaments are organized into functional units called ________.
why: The correct answer is: sarcomeres. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: The release of calcium ions initiates muscle contractions. Watch this video to learn more about the role of calcium. (a) What are “T-tubules” and what is their role? (b) Please also describe how actin-binding sites are made available for cross-bridging with myosin heads during contraction.
card.a: (a) The T-tubules are inward extensions of the sarcolemma that trigger the release of Ca⁺⁺ from SR during an Action Potential. (b) Ca⁺⁺ binds to troponin, and this slides the tropomyosin rods away from the binding sites.

card.q: How would muscle contractions be affected if skeletal muscle fibers did not have T-tubules?
card.a: Without T-tubules, action potential conduction into the interior of the cell would happen much more slowly, causing delays between neural stimulation and muscle contraction, resulting in slower, weaker contractions.

card.q: What causes the striated appearance of skeletal muscle tissue?
card.a: Dark A bands and light I bands repeat along myofibrils, and the alignment of myofibrils in the cell cause the entire cell to appear striated.

card.q: How would muscle contractions be affected if ATP was completely depleted in a muscle fiber?
card.a: Without ATP, the myosin heads cannot detach from the actin-binding sites. All of the “stuck” cross-bridges result in muscle stiffness. In a live person, this can cause a condition like “writer’s cramps.” In a recently dead person, it results in rigor mortis.

q: During which phase of a twitch in a muscle fiber is tension the greatest?
why: The correct answer is: contraction phase. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle contraction that shortens the muscle to move a load”
why: concentric contraction: muscle contraction that shortens the muscle to move a load

q: Which term matches this definition? “twitch contraction phase when tension increases”
why: contraction phase: twitch contraction phase when tension increases

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle contraction that lengthens the muscle as the tension is diminished”
why: eccentric contraction: muscle contraction that lengthens the muscle as the tension is diminished

q: Which term matches this definition? “modification of contraction strength”
why: graded muscle response: modification of contraction strength

q: Which term matches this definition? “abnormally high muscle tone”
why: hypertonia: abnormally high muscle tone

q: Which term matches this definition? “abnormally low muscle tone caused by the absence of low-level contractions”
why: hypotonia: abnormally low muscle tone caused by the absence of low-level contractions

card.q: Why does a motor unit of the eye have few muscle fibers compared to a motor unit of the leg?
card.a: Eyes require fine movements and a high degree of control, which is permitted by having fewer muscle fibers associated with a neuron.

card.q: What factors contribute to the amount of tension produced in an individual muscle fiber?
card.a: The length, size and types of muscle fiber and the frequency of neural stimulation contribute to the amount of tension produced in an individual muscle fiber.

q: Muscle fatigue is caused by ________.
options: buildup of ATP and lactic acid levels
exhaustion of energy reserves and buildup of lactic acid levels
buildup of ATP and pyruvic acid levels
exhaustion of energy reserves and buildup of pyruvic acid levels
why: The correct answer is: exhaustion of energy reserves and buildup of lactic acid levels. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A sprinter would experience muscle fatigue sooner than a marathon runner due to ________.
options: anaerobic metabolism in the muscles of the sprinter
anaerobic metabolism in the muscles of the marathon runner
aerobic metabolism in the muscles of the sprinter
glycolysis in the muscles of the marathon runner
why: The correct answer is: anaerobic metabolism in the muscles of the sprinter. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What aspect of creatine phosphate allows it to supply energy to muscles?
why: The correct answer is: phosphate bonds. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Drug X blocks ATP regeneration from ADP and phosphate. How will muscle cells respond to this drug?
options: by absorbing ATP from the bloodstream
by using ADP as an energy source
by using glycogen as an energy source
why: The correct answer is: none of the above. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle fiber that primarily uses anaerobic glycolysis”
why: fast glycolytic (FG): muscle fiber that primarily uses anaerobic glycolysis

q: Which term matches this definition? “intermediate muscle fiber that is between slow oxidative and fast glycolytic fibers”
why: fast oxidative (FO): intermediate muscle fiber that is between slow oxidative and fast glycolytic fibers

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle fiber that primarily uses aerobic respiration”
why: slow oxidative (SO): muscle fiber that primarily uses aerobic respiration

card.q: Why do muscle cells use creatine phosphate instead of glycolysis to supply ATP for the first few seconds of muscle contraction?
card.a: Creatine phosphate is used because creatine phosphate and ADP are converted very quickly into ATP by creatine kinase. Glycolysis cannot generate ATP as quickly as creatine phosphate.

card.q: Is aerobic respiration more or less efficient than glycolysis? Explain your answer.
card.a: Aerobic respiration is much more efficient than anaerobic glycolysis, yielding 36 ATP per molecule of glucose, as opposed to two ATP produced by glycolysis.

q: The muscles of a professional sprinter are most likely to have ________.
options: 80 percent fast-twitch muscle fibers and 20 percent slow-twitch muscle fibers
20 percent fast-twitch muscle fibers and 80 percent slow-twitch muscle fibers
50 percent fast-twitch muscle fibers and 50 percent slow-twitch muscle fibers
40 percent fast-twitch muscle fibers and 60 percent slow-twitch muscle fibers
why: The correct answer is: 80 percent fast-twitch muscle fibers and 20 percent slow-twitch muscle fibers. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The muscles of a professional marathon runner are most likely to have ________.
options: 80 percent fast-twitch muscle fibers and 20 percent slow-twitch muscle fibers
20 percent fast-twitch muscle fibers and 80 percent slow-twitch muscle fibers
50 percent fast-twitch muscle fibers and 50 percent slow-twitch muscle fibers
40 percent fast-twitch muscle fibers and 60 percent slow-twitch muscle fibers
why: The correct answer is: 20 percent fast-twitch muscle fibers and 80 percent slow-twitch muscle fibers. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following statements is true?
options: Fast fibers have a small diameter.
Fast fibers contain loosely packed myofibrils.
Fast fibers have large glycogen reserves.
why: The correct answer is: Fast fibers have large glycogen reserves.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following statements is false?
options: Slow fibers have a small network of capillaries.
Slow fibers contain the pigment myoglobin.
Slow fibers contain a large number of mitochondria.
Slow fibers contract for extended periods.
why: The correct answer is: Slow fibers have a small network of capillaries.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “formation of blood capillary networks”
why: angiogenesis: formation of blood capillary networks

q: Which term matches this definition? “loss of structural proteins from muscle fibers”
why: atrophy: loss of structural proteins from muscle fibers

q: Which term matches this definition? “addition of structural proteins to muscle fibers”
why: hypertrophy: addition of structural proteins to muscle fibers

q: Which term matches this definition? “age-related muscle atrophy”
why: sarcopenia: age-related muscle atrophy

card.q: What changes occur at the cellular level in response to endurance training?
card.a: Endurance training modifies slow fibers to make them more efficient by producing more mitochondria to enable more aerobic metabolism and more ATP production. Endurance exercise can also increase the amount of myoglobin in a cell and formation of more extensive capillary networks around the fiber.

card.q: What changes occur at the cellular level in response to resistance training?
card.a: Resistance exercises affect muscles by causing the formation of more actin and myosin, increasing the structure of muscle fibers.

q: Cardiac muscles differ from skeletal muscles in that they ________.
why: The correct answer is: contain intercalated discs. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: If cardiac muscle cells were prevented from undergoing aerobic metabolism, they ultimately would ________.
why: The correct answer is: stop contracting. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “heart’s ability to control its own contractions”
why: autorhythmicity: heart’s ability to control its own contractions

q: Which term matches this definition? “cell structure that anchors the ends of cardiac muscle fibers to allow contraction to occur”
why: desmosome: cell structure that anchors the ends of cardiac muscle fibers to allow contraction to occur

q: Which term matches this definition? “part of the sarcolemma that connects cardiac tissue, and contains gap junctions and desmosomes”
why: intercalated disc: part of the sarcolemma that connects cardiac tissue, and contains gap junctions and desmosomes

card.q: What would be the drawback of cardiac contractions being the same duration as skeletal muscle contractions?
card.a: An action potential could reach a cardiac muscle cell before it has entered the relaxation phase, resulting in the sustained contractions of tetanus. If this happened, the heart would not beat regularly.

card.q: How are cardiac muscle cells similar to and different from skeletal muscle cells?
card.a: Cardiac and skeletal muscle cells both contain ordered myofibrils and are striated. Cardiac muscle cells are branched and contain intercalated discs, which skeletal muscles do not have.

q: Smooth muscles differ from skeletal and cardiac muscles in that they ________.
why: The correct answer is: lack myofibrils. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following statements describes smooth muscle cells?
options: They have a rapid onset of contractions.
why: The correct answer is: They are resistant to fatigue.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “regulatory protein that facilitates contraction in smooth muscles”
why: calmodulin: regulatory protein that facilitates contraction in smooth muscles

q: Which term matches this definition? “sarcoplasmic structure that attaches to the sarcolemma and shortens the muscle as thin filaments slide past thick filaments”
why: dense body: sarcoplasmic structure that attaches to the sarcolemma and shortens the muscle as thin filaments slide past thick filaments

q: Which term matches this definition? “process in which one cell splits to produce new cells”
why: hyperplasia: process in which one cell splits to produce new cells

q: Which term matches this definition? “subset of a cross-bridge in which actin and myosin remain locked together”
why: latch-bridges: subset of a cross-bridge in which actin and myosin remain locked together

q: Which term matches this definition? “cell that triggers action potentials in smooth muscle”
why: pacesetter cell: cell that triggers action potentials in smooth muscle

q: Which term matches this definition? “relaxation of smooth muscle tissue after being stretched”
why: stress-relaxation response: relaxation of smooth muscle tissue after being stretched

card.q: Why can smooth muscles contract over a wider range of resting lengths than skeletal and cardiac muscle?
card.a: Smooth muscles can contract over a wider range of resting lengths because the actin and myosin filaments in smooth muscle are not as rigidly organized as those in skeletal and cardiac muscle.

card.q: Describe the differences between single-unit smooth muscle and multiunit smooth muscle.
card.a: Single-unit smooth muscle is found in the walls of hollow organs; multiunit smooth muscle is found in airways to the lungs and large arteries. Single-unit smooth muscle cells contract synchronously, they are coupled by gap junctions, and they exhibit spontaneous action potential. Multiunit smooth cells lack gap junctions, and their contractions are not synchronous.

q: From which embryonic cell type does muscle tissue develop?
why: The correct answer is: myoblast cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which cell type helps to repair injured muscle fibers?
why: The correct answer is: satellite cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “replacement of muscle fibers by scar tissue”
why: fibrosis: replacement of muscle fibers by scar tissue

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle-forming stem cell”
why: myoblast: muscle-forming stem cell

q: Which term matches this definition? “fusion of many myoblast cells”
why: myotube: fusion of many myoblast cells

q: Which term matches this definition? “stem cell that regenerates smooth muscle cells”
why: pericyte: stem cell that regenerates smooth muscle cells

q: Which term matches this definition? “stem cell that helps to repair muscle cells”
why: satellite cell: stem cell that helps to repair muscle cells

q: Which term matches this definition? “blocks of paraxial mesoderm cells”
why: somites: blocks of paraxial mesoderm cells

card.q: Why is muscle that has sustained significant damage unable to produce the same amount of power as it could before being damaged?
card.a: If the damage exceeds what can be repaired by satellite cells, the damaged tissue is replaced by scar tissue, which cannot contract.

card.q: Which muscle type(s) (skeletal, smooth, or cardiac) can regenerate new muscle cells/fibers? Explain your answer.
card.a: Smooth muscle tissue can regenerate from stem cells called pericytes, cells found in some small blood vessels. These allow smooth muscle cells to regenerate and repair much more readily than skeletal and cardiac muscle tissue.

q: Which of the following is unique to the muscles of facial expression?
options: They all originate from the scalp musculature.
They insert onto the cartilage found around the face.
They only insert onto the facial bones.
why: The correct answer is: They insert into the skin.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following helps an agonist work?
why: The correct answer is: a synergist. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following statements is correct about what happens during flexion?
options: The angle between bones is increased.
The angle between bones is decreased.
The bone moves away from the body.
The bone moves toward the center of the body.
why: The correct answer is: The angle between bones is decreased.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which is moved the least during muscle contraction?
why: The correct answer is: the origin. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which muscle has a convergent pattern of fascicles?
why: The correct answer is: pectoralis major. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A muscle that has a pattern of fascicles running along the long axis of the muscle has which of the following fascicle arrangements?
why: The correct answer is: parallel. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which arrangement best describes a bipennate muscle?
options: The muscle fibers feed in on an angle to a long tendon from both sides.
The muscle fibers feed in on an angle to a long tendon from all directions.
The muscle fibers feed in on an angle to a long tendon from one side.
The muscle fibers on one side of a tendon feed into it at a certain angle and muscle fibers on the other side of the tendon feed into it at the opposite angle.
why: The correct answer is: The muscle fibers feed in on an angle to a long tendon from both sides.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: What effect does fascicle arrangement have on a muscle’s action?
card.a: Fascicle arrangements determine what type of movement a muscle can make. For instance, circular muscles act as sphincters, closing orifices.

card.q: Movements of the body occur at joints. Describe how muscles are arranged around the joints of the body.
card.a: Muscles work in pairs to facilitate movement of the bones around the joints. Agonists are the prime movers while antagonists oppose or resist the movements of the agonists. Synergists assist the agonists, and fixators stabilize a muscle’s origin.

card.q: Explain how a synergist assists an agonist by being a fixator.
card.a: Agonists are the prime movers while antagonists oppose or resist the movements of the agonists. Synergists assist the agonists, and fixators stabilize a muscle’s origin.

q: The location of a muscle’s insertion and origin can determine ________.
options: the load a muscle can carry
why: The correct answer is: action. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Where is the temporalis muscle located?
options: on the side of the head
why: The correct answer is: on the side of the head. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which muscle name does not make sense?
why: The correct answer is: extensor minimus longus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following terms would be used in the name of a muscle that moves the leg away from the body?
why: The correct answer is: abductor. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “moves the bone away from the midline”
why: abductor: moves the bone away from the midline

q: Which term matches this definition? “moves the bone toward the midline”
why: adductor: moves the bone toward the midline

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle that increases the angle at the joint”
why: extensor: muscle that increases the angle at the joint

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle that decreases the angle at the joint”
why: flexor: muscle that decreases the angle at the joint

card.q: Describe the different criteria that contribute to how skeletal muscles are named.
card.a: In anatomy and physiology, many word roots are Latin or Greek. Portions, or roots, of the word give us clues about the function, shape, action, or location of a muscle.

q: Which of the following is a prime mover in head flexion?
why: The correct answer is: sternocleidomastoid. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Where is the inferior oblique muscle located?
why: The correct answer is: in the eye socket. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the action of the masseter?
why: The correct answer is: chewing. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The names of the extrinsic tongue muscles commonly end in ________.
why: The correct answer is: -glossus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the function of the erector spinae?
why: The correct answer is: postural support. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Explain the difference between axial and appendicular muscles.
card.a: Axial muscles originate on the axial skeleton (the bones in the head, neck, and core of the body), whereas appendicular muscles originate on the bones that make up the body’s limbs.

card.q: Describe the muscles of the anterior neck.
card.a: The muscles of the anterior neck are arranged to facilitate swallowing and speech. They work on the hyoid bone, with the suprahyoid muscles pulling up and the infrahyoid muscles pulling down.

card.q: Why are the muscles of the face different from typical skeletal muscle?
card.a: Most skeletal muscles create movement by actions on the skeleton. Facial muscles are different in that they create facial movements and expressions by pulling on the skin—no bone movements are involved.

q: Which of the following abdominal muscles is not a part of the anterior abdominal wall?
why: The correct answer is: quadratus lumborum. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which muscle pair plays a role in respiration?
why: The correct answer is: diaphragm, scalene. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the linea alba?
options: a small muscle that helps with compression of the abdominal organs
a long tendon that runs down the middle of the rectus abdominis
a long band of collagen fibers that connects the hip to the knee
another name for the tendinous inscription
why: The correct answer is: a long tendon that runs down the middle of the rectus abdominis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “posterior triangle of the perineum that includes the anus”
why: anal triangle: posterior triangle of the perineum that includes the anus

q: Which term matches this definition? “opening in the diaphragm that allows the inferior vena cava to pass through; foramen for the vena cava”
why: caval opening: opening in the diaphragm that allows the inferior vena cava to pass through; foramen for the vena cava

q: Which term matches this definition? “deep perineal muscle in females”
why: compressor urethrae: deep perineal muscle in females

q: Which term matches this definition? “deep perineal muscle in males”
why: deep transverse perineal: deep perineal muscle in males

q: Which term matches this definition? “skeletal muscle that separates the thoracic and abdominal cavities and is dome-shaped at rest”
why: diaphragm: skeletal muscle that separates the thoracic and abdominal cavities and is dome-shaped at rest

q: Which term matches this definition? “superficial intercostal muscles that raise the rib cage”
why: external intercostal: superficial intercostal muscles that raise the rib cage

card.q: Describe the fascicle arrangement in the muscles of the abdominal wall. How do they relate to each other?
card.a: Arranged into layers, the muscles of the abdominal wall are the internal and external obliques, which run on diagonals, the rectus abdominis, which runs straight down the midline of the body, and the transversus abdominis, which wraps across the trunk of the body.

card.q: What are some similarities and differences between the diaphragm and the pelvic diaphragm?
card.a: Both diaphragms are thin sheets of skeletal muscle that horizontally span areas of the trunk. The diaphragm separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities is the primary muscle of breathing. The pelvic diaphragm, consisting of two paired muscles, the coccygeus and the levator ani, forms the pelvic floor at the inferior end of the trunk.

q: The rhomboid major and minor muscles are deep to the ________.
why: The correct answer is: trapezius. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which muscle extends the forearm?
why: The correct answer is: triceps brachii. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the origin of the wrist flexors?
options: the lateral epicondyle of the humerus
the medial epicondyle of the humerus
the carpal bones of the wrist
the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus
why: The correct answer is: the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which muscles stabilize the pectoral girdle?
why: The correct answer is: axial and scapular. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle that abducts the little finger”
why: abductor digiti minimi: muscle that abducts the little finger

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle that adducts the thumb”
why: adductor pollicis: muscle that adducts the thumb

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle that abducts the thumb”
why: abductor pollicis brevis: muscle that abducts the thumb

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle that inserts into the first metacarpal”
why: abductor pollicis longus: muscle that inserts into the first metacarpal

q: Which term matches this definition? “small muscle on the lateral posterior elbow that extends the forearm”
why: anconeus: small muscle on the lateral posterior elbow that extends the forearm

q: Which term matches this definition? “(anterior flexor compartment of the arm) the biceps brachii, brachialis, brachioradialis, and their associated blood vessels and nerves”
options: superficial posterior compartment of the forearm
why: anterior compartment of the arm: (anterior flexor compartment of the arm) the biceps brachii, brachialis, brachioradialis, and their associated blood vessels and nerves

card.q: The tendons of which muscles form the rotator cuff? Why is the rotator cuff important?
card.a: Tendons of the infraspinatus, supraspinatus, teres minor, and the subscapularis form the rotator cuff, which forms a foundation on which the arms and shoulders can be stabilized and move.

card.q: List the general muscle groups of the shoulders and upper limbs as well as their subgroups.
card.a: The muscles that make up the shoulders and upper limbs include the muscles that position the pelvic girdle, the muscles that move the humerus, the muscles that move the forearm, and the muscles that move the wrists, hands, and fingers.

q: The large muscle group that attaches the leg to the pelvic girdle and produces extension of the hip joint is the ________ group.
why: The correct answer is: gluteal. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which muscle produces movement that allows you to cross your legs?
why: The correct answer is: the sartorius. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the largest muscle in the lower leg?
why: The correct answer is: gastrocnemius. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The vastus intermedius muscle is deep to which of the following muscles?
why: The correct answer is: rectus femoris. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle that adducts and medially rotates the thigh”
why: adductor brevis: muscle that adducts and medially rotates the thigh

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle that adducts, medially rotates, and flexes the thigh”
why: adductor longus: muscle that adducts, medially rotates, and flexes the thigh

q: Which term matches this definition? “muscle with an anterior fascicle that adducts, medially rotates and flexes the thigh, and a posterior fascicle that assists in thigh extension”
why: adductor magnus: muscle with an anterior fascicle that adducts, medially rotates and flexes the thigh, and a posterior fascicle that assists in thigh extension

q: Which term matches this definition? “region that includes muscles that dorsiflex the foot”
why: anterior compartment of the leg: region that includes muscles that dorsiflex the foot

q: Which term matches this definition? “region that includes muscles that flex the thigh and extend the leg”
why: anterior compartment of the thigh: region that includes muscles that flex the thigh and extend the leg

q: Which term matches this definition? “(also, Achilles tendon) strong tendon that inserts into the calcaneal bone of the ankle”
why: calcaneal tendon: (also, Achilles tendon) strong tendon that inserts into the calcaneal bone of the ankle

card.q: Which muscles form the hamstrings? How do they function together?
card.a: The biceps femoris, semimembranosus, and semitendinosus form the hamstrings. The hamstrings flex the leg at the knee joint.

card.q: Which muscles form the quadriceps? How do they function together?
card.a: The rectus femoris, vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, and vastus intermedius form the quadriceps. The quadriceps muscles extend the leg at the knee joint.

q: Which of the following cavities contains a component of the central nervous system?
why: The correct answer is: cranial. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which structure predominates in the white matter of the brain?
options: bundles of dendrites from the enteric nervous system
why: The correct answer is: myelinated axons. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which part of a neuron transmits an electrical signal to a target cell?
why: The correct answer is: axon. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term describes a bundle of axons in the peripheral nervous system?
why: The correct answer is: nerve. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which functional division of the nervous system would be responsible for the physiological changes seen during exercise (e.g., increased heart rate and sweating)?
why: The correct answer is: autonomic. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Visit this site to read about a woman that notices that her daughter is having trouble walking up the stairs. This leads to the discovery of a hereditary condition that affects the brain and spinal cord. The electromyography and MRI tests indicated deficiencies in the spinal cord and cerebellum, both of which are responsible for controlling coordinated movements. To what functional division of the nervous system would these structures belong?
card.a: They are part of the somatic nervous system, which is responsible for voluntary movements such as walking or climbing the stairs.

card.q: What responses are generated by the nervous system when you run on a treadmill? Include an example of each type of tissue that is under nervous system control.
card.a: Running on a treadmill involves contraction of the skeletal muscles in the legs, increase in contraction of the cardiac muscle of the heart, and the production and secretion of sweat in the skin to stay cool.

card.q: When eating food, what anatomical and functional divisions of the nervous system are involved in the perceptual experience?
card.a: The sensation of taste associated with eating is sensed by nerves in the periphery that are involved in sensory and somatic functions.

q: What type of glial cell provides myelin for the axons in a tract?
why: The correct answer is: oligodendrocyte. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which part of a neuron contains the nucleus?
why: The correct answer is: soma. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following substances is least able to cross the blood-brain barrier?
why: The correct answer is: white blood cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What type of glial cell is the resident macrophage behind the blood-brain barrier?
why: The correct answer is: microglia. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What two types of macromolecules are the main components of myelin?
why: The correct answer is: lipids and proteins. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: The neurons are dynamic cells with the ability to make a vast number of connections and to respond incredibly quickly to stimuli and to initiate movements based on those stimuli. They are the focus of intense research as failures in physiology can lead to devastating illnesses. Why are neurons only found in animals? Why wouldn’t they be helpful for plants or microorganisms?
card.a: Neurons enable thought, perception, and movement. Plants do not move, so they do not need this type of tissue. Microorganisms are too small to have a nervous system. Many are single-celled, and therefore have organelles for perception and movement.

card.q: Multiple sclerosis is a demyelinating disease affecting the central nervous system. What type of cell would be the most likely target of this disease? Why?
card.a: The disease would target oligodendrocytes. In the CNS, oligodendrocytes provide the myelin for axons.

card.q: Which type of neuron, based on its shape, is best suited for relaying information directly from one neuron to another? Explain why.
card.a: Bipolar cells, because they have one dendrite that receives input and one axon that provides output, would be a direct relay between two other cells.

q: If a thermoreceptor is sensitive to temperature sensations, what would a chemoreceptor be sensitive to?
why: The correct answer is: molecules. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of these locations is where the greatest level of integration is taking place in the example of testing the temperature of the shower?
why: The correct answer is: cerebral cortex. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: How long does all the signaling through the sensory pathway, within the central nervous system, and through the motor command pathway take?
why: The correct answer is: fraction of a second. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the target of an upper motor neuron?
why: The correct answer is: lower motor neuron. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “change in voltage of a cell membrane in response to a stimulus that results in transmission of an electrical signal; unique to neurons and muscle fibers”
why: action potential: change in voltage of a cell membrane in response to a stimulus that results in transmission of an electrical signal; unique to neurons and muscle fibers

q: Which term matches this definition? “outermost layer of gray matter in the brain, where conscious perception takes place”
why: cerebral cortex: outermost layer of gray matter in the brain, where conscious perception takes place

q: Which term matches this definition? “change in the membrane potential that varies in size, depending on the size of the stimulus that elicits it”
why: graded potential: change in the membrane potential that varies in size, depending on the size of the stimulus that elicits it

q: Which term matches this definition? “second neuron in the motor command pathway that is directly connected to the skeletal muscle”
why: lower motor neuron: second neuron in the motor command pathway that is directly connected to the skeletal muscle

q: Which term matches this definition? “chemical signal that is released from the synaptic end bulb of a neuron to cause a change in the target cell”
why: neurotransmitter: chemical signal that is released from the synaptic end bulb of a neuron to cause a change in the target cell

q: Which term matches this definition? “region of the cerebral cortex responsible for generating motor commands, where the upper motor neuron cell body is located”
options: precentral gyrus of the frontal cortex
why: precentral gyrus of the frontal cortex: region of the cerebral cortex responsible for generating motor commands, where the upper motor neuron cell body is located

card.q: Sensory fibers, or pathways, are referred to as “afferent.” Motor fibers, or pathways, are referred to as “efferent.” What can you infer about the meaning of these two terms (afferent and efferent) in a structural or anatomical context?
card.a: Afferent means “toward,” as in sensory information traveling from the periphery into the CNS. Efferent means “away from,” as in motor commands that travel from the brain down the spinal cord and out into the periphery.

card.q: If a person has a motor disorder and cannot move their arm voluntarily, but their muscles have tone, which motor neuron—upper or lower—is probably affected? Explain why.
card.a: The upper motor neuron would be affected because it is carrying the command from the brain down.

q: What ion enters a neuron causing depolarization of the cell membrane?
why: The correct answer is: sodium. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open upon reaching what state?
why: The correct answer is: threshold. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What does a ligand-gated channel require in order to open?
options: increase in concentration of Na⁺ ions
increase in concentration of K⁺ ions
why: The correct answer is: binding of a neurotransmitter. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What does a mechanically gated channel respond to?
why: The correct answer is: physical stimulus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following voltages would most likely be measured during the relative refractory period?
why: The correct answer is: -80 mv. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is probably going to propagate an action potential fastest?
why: The correct answer is: a thick, myelinated axon. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: What happens across the membrane of an electrically active cell is a dynamic process that is hard to visualize with static images or through text descriptions. View this animation to really understand the process. What is the difference between the driving force for Na⁺ and K⁺? And what is similar about the movement of these two ions?
card.a: Sodium is moving into the cell because of the immense concentration gradient, whereas potassium is moving out because of the depolarization that sodium causes. However, they both move down their respective gradients, toward equilibrium.

card.q: What does it mean for an action potential to be an “all or none” event?
card.a: The cell membrane must reach threshold before voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open. If threshold is not reached, those channels do not open, and the depolarizing phase of the action potential does not occur, the cell membrane will just go back to its resting state.

card.q: The conscious perception of pain is often delayed because of the time it takes for the sensations to reach the cerebral cortex. Why would this be the case based on propagation of the axon potential?
card.a: Axons of pain sensing sensory neurons are thin and unmyelinated so that it takes longer for that sensation to reach the brain than other sensations.

q: How much of a change in the membrane potential is necessary for the summation of postsynaptic potentials to result in an action potential being generated?
why: The correct answer is: +15 mV. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A channel opens on a postsynaptic membrane that causes a negative ion to enter the cell. What type of graded potential is this?
why: The correct answer is: hyperpolarizing. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction?
why: The correct answer is: acetylcholine. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What type of receptor requires an effector protein to initiate a signal?
why: The correct answer is: metabotropic receptor. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following neurotransmitters is associated with inhibition exclusively?
why: The correct answer is: GABA. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Watch this video to learn about summation. The process of converting electrical signals to chemical signals and back requires subtle changes that can result in transient increases or decreases in membrane voltage. To cause a lasting change in the target cell, multiple signals are usually added together, or summated. Does spatial summation have to happen all at once, or can the separate signals arrive on the postsynaptic neuron at slightly different times? Explain your answer.
card.a: A second signal from a separate presynaptic neuron can arrive slightly later, as long as it arrives before the first one dies off, or dissipates.

card.q: If a postsynaptic cell has synapses from five different cells, and three cause EPSPs and two of them cause IPSPs, give an example of a series of depolarizations and hyperpolarizations that would result in the neuron reaching threshold.
card.a: EPSP1 = +5 mV, EPSP2 = +7 mV, EPSP 3 = +10 mV, IPSP1 = -4 mV, IPSP2 = -3 mV. 5 + 7 + 10 – 4 – 3 = +15 mV.

card.q: Why is the receptor the important element determining the effect a neurotransmitter has on a target cell?
card.a: Different neurotransmitters have different receptors. Thus, the type of receptor in the postsynaptic cell is what determines which ion channels open. Acetylcholine binding to the nicotinic receptor causes cations to cross the membrane. GABA binding to its receptor causes the anion chloride to cross the membrane.

q: Aside from the nervous system, which other organ system develops out of the ectoderm?
why: The correct answer is: integumentary. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which primary vesicle of the embryonic nervous system does not differentiate into more vesicles at the secondary stage?
why: The correct answer is: mesencephalon. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which adult structure(s) arises from the diencephalon?
why: The correct answer is: thalamus, hypothalamus, retina. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which non-nervous tissue develops from the neuroectoderm?
why: The correct answer is: craniofacial bone. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which structure is associated with the embryologic development of the peripheral nervous system?
why: The correct answer is: neural crest. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Watch this video to learn more about overall brain development in children, including the role of white matter and its contribution to cognitive function. The video focuses on forming connections in the brain, especially from birth to 30 years of age and it shows several MRI studies.
card.a: This is really a matter of opinion, but there are ethical issues to consider when a teenager’s behavior results in legal trouble.

card.q: Studying the embryonic development of the nervous system makes it easier to understand the complexity of the adult nervous system. Give one example of how development in the embryonic nervous system explains a more complex structure in the adult nervous system.
card.a: The retina, a PNS structure in the adult, grows from the diencephalon in the embryonic nervous system. The mature connections from the retina through the optic nerve/tract are to the hypothalamus and thalamus of the diencephalon, and to the midbrain, which developed directly adjacent to the diencephalon as the mesencephalon in the embryo.

card.q: What happens in development that suggests that there is a special relationship between the skeletal structure of the head and the nervous system?
card.a: The neural crest gives rise to PNS structures (such as ganglia) and also to cartilage and bone of the face and cranium.

q: Which lobe of the cerebral cortex is responsible for generating motor commands?
why: The correct answer is: frontal. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What region of the diencephalon coordinates homeostasis?
why: The correct answer is: hypothalamus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What level of the brain stem is the major input to the cerebellum?
why: The correct answer is: pons. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What region of the spinal cord contains motor neurons that direct the movement of skeletal muscles?
why: The correct answer is: anterior horn. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Brodmann’s areas map different regions of the ________ to particular functions.
why: The correct answer is: cerebral cortex. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Watch this video to learn about the basal nuclei (also known as the basal ganglia), which have two pathways that process information within the cerebrum. As shown in this video, the direct pathway is the shorter pathway through the system that results in increased activity in the cerebral cortex and increased motor activity. The direct pathway is described as resulting in “disinhibition” of the thalamus. What does disinhibition mean? What are the two neurons doing individually to cause this?
card.a: Both cells are inhibitory. The first cell inhibits the second one. Therefore, the second cell can no longer inhibit its target. This is disinhibition of that target across two synapses.

card.q: Damage to specific regions of the cerebral cortex, such as through a stroke, can result in specific losses of function. What functions would likely be lost by a stroke in the temporal lobe?
card.a: The temporal lobe has sensory functions associated with hearing and vision, as well as being important for memory. A stroke in the temporal lobe can result in specific sensory deficits in these systems (known as agnosias) or losses in memory.

card.q: Why do the anatomical inputs to the cerebellum suggest that it can compare motor commands and sensory feedback?
card.a: A copy of descending input from the cerebrum to the spinal cord, through the pons, and sensory feedback from the spinal cord and special senses like balance, through the medulla, both go to the cerebellum. It can therefore send output through the midbrain that will correct spinal cord control of skeletal muscle movements.

q: What blood vessel enters the cranium to supply the brain with fresh, oxygenated blood?
why: The correct answer is: internal carotid artery. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which layer of the meninges surrounds and supports the sinuses that form the route through which blood drains from the CNS?
why: The correct answer is: dura mater. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What type of glial cell is responsible for filtering blood to produce CSF at the choroid plexus?
why: The correct answer is: ependymal cell. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which portion of the ventricular system is found within the diencephalon?
why: The correct answer is: third ventricle. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What condition causes a stroke?
options: disruption of blood to the brain
why: The correct answer is: disruption of blood to the brain. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Watch this video that describes the procedure known as the lumbar puncture, a medical procedure used to sample the CSF. Because of the anatomy of the CNS, it is a relative safe location to insert a needle. Why is the lumbar puncture performed in the lower lumbar area of the vertebral column?
card.a: The spinal cord ends in the upper lumbar area of the vertebral column, so a needle inserted lower than that will not damage the nervous tissue of the CNS.

card.q: Watch this animation that shows the flow of CSF through the brain and spinal cord, and how it originates from the ventricles and then spreads into the space within the meninges, where the fluids then move into the venous sinuses to return to the cardiovascular circulation. What are the structures that produce CSF and where are they found? How are the structures indicated in this animation?
card.a: The choroid plexuses of the ventricles make CSF. As shown, there is a little of the blue color appearing in each ventricle that is joined by the color flowing from the other ventricles.

card.q: Why can the circle of Willis maintain perfusion of the brain even if there is a blockage in one part of the structure?
card.a: The structure is a circular connection of blood vessels, so that blood coming up from one of the arteries can flow in either direction around the circle and avoid any blockage or narrowing of the blood vessels.

card.q: Meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges that can have severe effects on neurological function. Why is infection of this structure potentially so dangerous?
card.a: The nerves that connect the periphery to the CNS pass through these layers of tissue and can be damaged by that inflammation, causing a loss of important neurological functions.

q: What type of ganglion contains neurons that control homeostatic mechanisms of the body?
why: The correct answer is: autonomic ganglion. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which ganglion is responsible for cutaneous sensations of the face?
why: The correct answer is: trigeminal ganglion. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the name for a bundle of axons within a nerve?
why: The correct answer is: fascicle. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which cranial nerve does not control functions in the head and neck?
why: The correct answer is: vagus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of these structures is not under direct control of the peripheral nervous system?
why: The correct answer is: gastric plexus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: If you zoom in on the DRG, you can see smaller satellite glial cells surrounding the large cell bodies of the sensory neurons. From what structure do satellite cells derive during embryologic development?
card.a: They derive from the neural crest.

card.q: To what structures in a skeletal muscle are the endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium comparable?
card.a: The endoneurium surrounding individual nerve fibers is comparable to the endomysium surrounding myofibrils, the perineurium bundling axons into fascicles is comparable to the perimysium bundling muscle fibers into fascicles, and the epineurium surrounding the whole nerve is comparable to the epimysium surrounding the muscle.

card.q: Why are ganglia and nerves not surrounded by protective structures like the meninges of the CNS?
card.a: The peripheral nervous tissues are out in the body, sometimes part of other organ systems. There is not a privileged blood supply like there is to the brain and spinal cord, so peripheral nervous tissues do not need the same sort of protections.

card.q: Testing for neurological function involves a series of tests of functions associated with the cranial nerves. What functions, and therefore which nerves, are being tested by asking a patient to follow the tip of a pen with their eyes?
card.a: The contraction of extraocular muscles is being tested, which is the function of the oculomotor, trochlear, and abducens nerves.

q: What type of receptor cell is responsible for transducing pain stimuli?
why: The correct answer is: nociceptor. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of these cranial nerves is part of the gustatory system?
why: The correct answer is: facial. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which submodality of taste is sensitive to the pH of saliva?
why: The correct answer is: sour. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Axons from which neuron in the retina make up the optic nerve?
why: The correct answer is: retinal ganglion cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What type of receptor cell is involved in the sensations of sound and balance?
why: The correct answer is: mechanoreceptor. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: The basilar membrane is the thin membrane that extends from the central core of the cochlea to the edge. What is anchored to this membrane so that they can be activated by movement of the fluids within the cochlea?
card.a: The hair cells are located in the organ of Corti, which is located on the basilar membrane. The stereocilia of those cells would normally be attached to the tectorial membrane (though they are detached in the micrograph because of processing of the tissue).

card.q: Watch this video to learn more about how the structures of the ear convert sound waves into a neural signal by moving the “hairs,” or stereocilia, of the cochlear duct. Specific locations along the length of the duct encode specific frequencies, or pitches. The brain interprets the meaning of the sounds we hear as music, speech, noise, etc. Which ear structures are responsible for the amplification and transfer of sound from the external ear to the inner ear?
card.a: The small bones in the middle ear, the ossicles, amplify and transfer sound between the tympanic membrane of the external ear and the oval window of the inner ear.

card.q: Watch this animation to learn more about the inner ear and to see the cochlea unroll, with the base at the back of the image and the apex at the front. Specific wavelengths of sound cause specific regions of the basilar membrane to vibrate, much like the keys of a piano produce sound at different frequencies. Based on the animation, where do frequencies—from high to low pitches—cause activity in the hair cells within the cochlear duct?
card.a: High frequencies activate hair cells toward the base of the cochlea, and low frequencies activate hair cells toward the apex of the cochlea.

card.q: The sweetener known as stevia can replace glucose in food. What does the molecular similarity of stevia to glucose mean for the gustatory sense?
card.a: The stevia molecule is similar to glucose such that it will bind to the glucose receptor in sweet-sensitive taste buds. However, it is not a substrate for the ATP-generating metabolism within cells.

card.q: Why does the blind spot from the optic disc in either eye not result in a blind spot in the visual field?
card.a: The visual field for each eye is projected onto the retina as light is focused by the lens. The visual information from the right visual field falls on the left side of the retina and vice versa. The optic disc in the right eye is on the medial side of the fovea, which would be the left side of the retina. However, the optic disc in the left eye would be on the right side of that fovea, so the right visual field falls on the side of the retina in the left field where there is no blind spot.

q: Which of these sensory modalities does not pass through the ventral posterior thalamus?
why: The correct answer is: audition. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which nucleus in the medulla is connected to the inferior colliculus?
why: The correct answer is: cochlear nucleus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Visual stimuli in the upper-left visual field will be processed in what region of the primary visual cortex?
why: The correct answer is: inferior right. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which location on the body has the largest region of somatosensory cortex representing it, according to the sensory homunculus?
why: The correct answer is: lips. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is a direct target of the vestibular ganglion?
why: The correct answer is: cerebellum. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: The inability to recognize people by their faces is a troublesome problem. It can be caused by trauma, or it may be inborn. Watch this video to learn more about a person who lost the ability to recognize faces as the result of an injury. She cannot recognize the faces of close family members or herself. What other information can a person suffering from prosopagnosia use to figure out whom they are seeing?
card.a: Even if a person cannot recognize a person’s face, other cues such as clothing, hairstyle, or a particular feature such as a prominent nose or facial hair, can help make an identification.

card.q: Following a motorcycle accident, the victim loses the ability to move the right leg but has normal control over the left one, suggesting a hemisection somewhere in the thoracic region of the spinal cord. What sensory deficits would be expected in terms of touch versus pain? Explain your answer.
card.a: The right leg would feel painful stimuli, but not touch, because the spinothalamic tract decussates at the level of entry, which would be below the injury, whereas the dorsal column system does not decussate until reaching the brain stem, which would be above the injury and thus those fibers would be damaged.

card.q: A pituitary tumor can cause perceptual losses in the lateral visual field. The pituitary gland is located directly inferior to the hypothalamus. Why would this happen?
card.a: As the tumor enlarges, it would press against the optic chiasm, and fibers from the medial retina would be disrupted. These fibers carry information about the lateral visual field because the visual scene is reversed as the light passes through the pupil and lens.

q: Which region of the frontal lobe is responsible for initiating movement by directly connecting to cranial and spinal motor neurons?
why: The correct answer is: primary motor cortex. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which extrapyramidal tract incorporates equilibrium sensations with motor commands to aid in posture and movement?
why: The correct answer is: vestibulospinal tract. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which region of gray matter in the spinal cord contains motor neurons that innervate skeletal muscles?
why: The correct answer is: ventral horn. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What type of reflex can protect the foot when a painful stimulus is sensed?
why: The correct answer is: withdrawal reflex. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the name for the topographical representation of the sensory input to the somatosensory cortex?
why: The correct answer is: homunculus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Watch this video to learn more about the descending motor pathway for the somatic nervous system. The autonomic connections are mentioned, which are covered in another chapter. From this brief video, only some of the descending motor pathway of the somatic nervous system is described. Which division of the pathway is described and which division is left out?
card.a: The video only describes the lateral division of the corticospinal tract. The anterior division is omitted.

card.q: Watch this video to learn more about the reflex arc of the corneal reflex. When the right cornea senses a tactile stimulus, what happens to the left eye? Explain your answer.
card.a: The left eye also blinks. The sensory input from one eye activates the motor response of both eyes so that they both blink.

card.q: The prefrontal lobotomy is a drastic—and largely out-of-practice—procedure used to disconnect that portion of the cerebral cortex from the rest of the frontal lobe and the diencephalon as a psychiatric therapy. Why would this have been thought necessary for someone with a potentially uncontrollable behavior?
card.a: The prefrontal cortex is involved in decision-making functions that lead to motor responses through connections to the more posterior motor regions. These early aspects of behavior are often associated with a person’s personality, so disrupting those connections will lead to severe changes in behavior.

card.q: If a reflex is a limited circuit within the somatic system, why do physical and neurological exams include them to test the health of an individual?
card.a: Though reflexes are simple circuits within the nervous system, they are representative of the more involved circuits of the somatic nervous system and can be used to quickly assess the state of neurological function for a person.

q: Which of these physiological changes would not be considered part of the sympathetic fight-or-flight response?
why: The correct answer is: increased stomach motility. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which type of fiber could be considered the longest?
why: The correct answer is: preganglionic parasympathetic. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which signaling molecule is most likely responsible for an increase in digestive activity?
why: The correct answer is: acetylcholine. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of these cranial nerves contains preganglionic parasympathetic fibers?
why: The correct answer is: facial, CN VII. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is not a target of a sympathetic preganglionic fiber?
why: The correct answer is: intermural ganglion. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: In the context of a lioness hunting on the savannah, why would the sympathetic system not activate the digestive system?
card.a: Whereas energy is needed for running away from the threat, blood needs to be sent to the skeletal muscles for oxygen supply. The additional fuel, in the form of carbohydrates, probably wouldn’t improve the ability to escape the threat as much as the diversion of oxygen-rich blood would hinder it.

card.q: A target effector, such as the heart, receives input from the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems. What is the actual difference between the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions at the level of those connections (i.e., at the synapse)?
card.a: The postganglionic sympathetic fiber releases norepinephrine, whereas the postganglionic parasympathetic fiber releases acetylcholine. Specific locations in the heart have adrenergic receptors and muscarinic receptors. Which receptors are bound is the signal that determines how the heart responds.

q: Which of the following represents a sensory input that is not part of both the somatic and autonomic systems?
why: The correct answer is: baroreception. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the term for a reflex that does not include a CNS component?
why: The correct answer is: short reflex. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What neurotransmitter will result in constriction of the pupil?
why: The correct answer is: acetylcholine. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What gland produces a secretion that causes fight-or-flight responses in effectors?
why: The correct answer is: adrenal medulla. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is an incorrect pairing?
why: The correct answer is: acetylcholine decreases digestion. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Read this article to learn about a teenager who experiences a series of spells that suggest a stroke. He undergoes endless tests and seeks input from multiple doctors. In the end, one expert, one question, and a simple blood pressure cuff answers the question. Why would the heart have to beat faster when the teenager changes his body position from lying down to sitting, and then to standing?
card.a: The effect of gravity on circulation means that it is harder to get blood up from the legs as the body takes on a vertical orientation.

card.q: Watch this video to learn about the pupillary reflexes. The pupillary light reflex involves sensory input through the optic nerve and motor response through the oculomotor nerve to the ciliary ganglion, which projects to the circular fibers of the iris. As shown in this short animation, pupils will constrict to limit the amount of light falling on the retina under bright lighting conditions. What constitutes the afferent and efferent branches of the competing reflex (dilation)?
card.a: The optic nerve still carries the afferent input, but the output is from the thoracic spinal cord, through the superior cervical ganglion, to the radial fibers of the iris.

card.q: Damage to internal organs will present as pain associated with a particular surface area of the body. Why would something like irritation to the diaphragm, which is between the thoracic and abdominal cavities, feel like pain in the shoulder or neck?
card.a: The nerves that carry sensory information from the diaphragm enter the spinal cord in the cervical region where somatic sensory fibers from the shoulder and neck would enter. The brain superimposes this experience onto the sensory homunculus where the somatic nerves are connected.

card.q: Medical practice is paying more attention to the autonomic system in considering disease states. Why would autonomic tone be important in considering cardiovascular disease?
card.a: Within the cardiovascular system, different aspects demonstrate variation in autonomic tone. Heart rate is under parasympathetic tone, and blood pressure is under sympathetic tone. Pharmaceuticals that treat cardiovascular disorders may be more effective if they work with the normal state of the autonomic system. Alternatively, some disorders may be exacerbated by autonomic deficits and common therapies might not be as effective.

q: Which of these locations in the forebrain is the master control center for homeostasis through the autonomic and endocrine systems?
why: The correct answer is: hypothalamus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which nerve projects to the hypothalamus to indicate the level of light stimuli in the retina?
why: The correct answer is: optic. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What region of the limbic lobe is responsible for generating stress responses via the hypothalamus?
why: The correct answer is: amygdala. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is another name for the preganglionic sympathetic fibers that project to the heart?
why: The correct answer is: cardiac accelerator nerve. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What central fiber tract connects forebrain and brain stem structures with the hypothalamus?
why: The correct answer is: medial forebrain bundle. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Horner’s syndrome is a condition that presents with changes in one eye, such as pupillary constriction and dropping of eyelids, as well as decreased sweating in the face. Why could a tumor in the thoracic cavity have an effect on these autonomic functions?
card.a: Pupillary dilation and sweating, two functions lost in Horner’s syndrome, are caused by the sympathetic system. A tumor in the thoracic cavity may interrupt the output of the thoracic ganglia that project to the head and face.

card.q: The cardiovascular center is responsible for regulating the heart and blood vessels through homeostatic mechanisms. What tone does each component of the cardiovascular system have? What connections does the cardiovascular center invoke to keep these two systems in their resting tone?
card.a: The heart—based on the resting heart rate—is under parasympathetic tone, and the blood vessels—based on the lack of parasympathetic input—are under sympathetic tone. The vagus nerve contributes to the lowered resting heart rate, whereas the vasomotor nerves maintain the slight constriction of systemic blood vessels.

q: A drug that affects both divisions of the autonomic system is going to bind to, or block, which type of neurotransmitter receptor?
why: The correct answer is: nicotinic. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A drug is called an agonist if it ________.
options: acts like the endogenous neurotransmitter by binding to its receptor
blocks the voltage-gated calcium ion channel
why: The correct answer is: acts like the endogenous neurotransmitter by binding to its receptor. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which type of drug would be an antidote to atropine poisoning?
why: The correct answer is: muscarinic agonist. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which kind of drug would have anti-anxiety effects?
why: The correct answer is: α-blocker. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which type of drug could be used to treat asthma by opening airways wider?
why: The correct answer is: sympathomimetic drug. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Watch this video to learn about the side effects of 3-D movies. As discussed in this video, movies that are shot in 3-D can cause motion sickness, which elicits the autonomic symptoms of nausea and sweating. The disconnection between the perceived motion on the screen and the lack of any change in equilibrium stimulates these symptoms. Why do you think sitting close to the screen or right in the middle of the theater makes motion sickness during a 3-D movie worse?
card.a: When the visual field is completely taken up by the movie, the brain is confused by the lack of vestibular stimuli to match the visual stimuli. Sitting to the side, or so that the edges of the screen can be seen, will help by providing a stable visual cue along with the magic of the cinematic experience.

card.q: Why does smoking increase the risk of heart disease? Provide two reasons based on autonomic function.
card.a: Blood vessels, and therefore blood pressure, are primarily influenced by only the sympathetic system. There is no parasympathetic influence on blood pressure, so nicotine activation of autonomic ganglia will preferentially increase blood pressure. Also, cardiac muscle tissue is only modulated by autonomic inputs, so the conflicting information from both sympathetic and parasympathetic postganglionic fibers will cause arrhythmias. Both hypertension and arrhythmias are cardiac risk factors.

card.q: Why might topical, cosmetic application of atropine or scopolamine from the belladonna plant not cause fatal poisoning, as would occur with ingestion of the plant?
card.a: Drops of these substances into the eyes, as was once done cosmetically, blocks the muscarinic receptors in the smooth muscle of the iris. The concentration of this direct application is probably below the concentration that would cause poisoning if it got into the bloodstream. The possibility of that concentration being wrong and causing poisoning is too great, however, for atropine to be used as a cosmetic.

q: Which major section of the neurological exam is most likely to reveal damage to the cerebellum?
why: The correct answer is: coordination exam. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What function would most likely be affected by a restriction of a blood vessel in the cerebral cortex?
why: The correct answer is: language. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which major section of the neurological exam includes subtests that are sometimes considered a separate set of tests concerned with walking?
why: The correct answer is: coordination exam. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Memory, emotional, language, and sensorimotor deficits together are most likely the result of what kind of damage?
why: The correct answer is: developmental disorder. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Where is language function localized in the majority of people?
why: The correct answer is: left cerebral hemisphere. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Watch this video that provides a demonstration of the neurological exam—a series of tests that can be performed rapidly when a patient is initially brought into an emergency department. The exam can be repeated on a regular basis to keep a record of how and if neurological function changes over time. In what order were the sections of the neurological exam tested in this video, and which section seemed to be left out?
card.a: Coordination and gait were tested first, followed by mental status, motor, sensory, and reflexes. There were no specific tests of the cranial nerves.

card.q: Why is a rapid assessment of neurological function important in an emergency situation?
card.a: If an ischemic event has occurred, nervous tissue may be compromised, but quick intervention—possibly within a few hours—may be the critical aspect of recovery.

card.q: How is the diagnostic category of TIA different from a stroke?
card.a: The main difference between a stroke and TIA is time. If the result of a cerebrovascular accident lasts longer than 24 hours, then it is considered a stroke. Otherwise, it is considered transient and is labeled a TIA.

q: Which of the following could be elements of cytoarchitecture, as related to Brodmann’s microscopic studies of the cerebral cortex?
options: number of neurons per square millimeter
why: The correct answer is: number of neurons per square millimeter. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following could be a multimodal integrative area?
why: The correct answer is: Wernicke’s area. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which is an example of episodic memory?
options: needing to wear an oven mitt to take a cake out of the oven
why: The correct answer is: your last birthday party. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which type of aphasia is more like hearing a foreign language spoken?
why: The correct answer is: receptive aphasia. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What region of the cerebral cortex is associated with understanding language, both from another person and the language a person generates himself or herself?
why: The correct answer is: superior temporal gyrus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: A patient’s performance of the majority of the mental status exam subtests is in line with the expected norms, but the patient cannot repeat a string of numbers given by the examiner. What is a likely explanation?
card.a: The patient has suffered a stroke to the prefrontal cortex where working memory is localized.

card.q: A patient responds to the question “What is your name?” with a look of incomprehension. Which of the two major language areas is most likely affected and what is the name for that type of aphasia?
card.a: Wernicke’s area is associated with the comprehension of language, so the person probably doesn’t understand the question being asked and cannot respond meaningfully. This is called a receptive aphasia.

q: Without olfactory sensation to complement gustatory stimuli, food will taste bland unless it is seasoned with which substance?
why: The correct answer is: salt. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following cranial nerves is not part of the VOR?
why: The correct answer is: optic. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which nerve is responsible for controlling the muscles that result in the gag reflex?
why: The correct answer is: vagus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which nerve is responsible for taste, as well as salivation, in the anterior oral cavity?
why: The correct answer is: facial. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following nerves controls movements of the neck?
why: The correct answer is: spinal accessory. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: As a person ages, their ability to focus on near objects (accommodation) changes. If a person is already myopic (near-sighted), why would corrective lenses not be necessary to read a book or computer screen?
