card.a: If the person already has problems focusing on far objects, and wears corrective lenses to see farther objects, then as accommodation changes, focusing on a reading surface might still be in their naturally near-sighted range.

card.q: When a patient flexes their neck, the head tips to the right side. Also, their tongue sticks out slightly to the left when they try to stick it straight out. Where is the damage to the brain stem most likely located?
card.a: The medulla is where the accessory nerve, which controls the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and the hypoglossal nerve, which controls the genioglossus muscle, are both located. The weakness of the left side of the neck, and the tendency of the tongue to point to that side, both show that the damage is on the left side of the brain stem.

q: Which of the following is not part of the corticospinal pathway?
why: The correct answer is: cerebellar deep white matter. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which subtest is directed at proprioceptive sensation?
why: The correct answer is: Romberg test. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What term describes the inability to lift the arm above the level of the shoulder?
why: The correct answer is: paresis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which type of reflex is the jaw-jerk reflex that is part of the cranial nerve exam for the vestibulocochlear nerve?
why: The correct answer is: stretch reflex. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is a feature of both somatic and visceral senses?
options: projects to a ganglion near the target effector
involves an axon in the ventral nerve root
why: The correct answer is: involves an axon in the ventral nerve root. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Watch this video to see how to test reflexes in the abdomen. Testing reflexes of the trunk is not commonly performed in the neurological exam, but if findings suggest a problem with the thoracic segments of the spinal cord, a series of superficial reflexes of the abdomen can localize function to those segments. If contraction is not observed when the skin lateral to the umbilicus (belly button) is stimulated, what level of the spinal cord may be damaged?
card.a: The region lateral to the umbilicus is innervated by T9–T11, approximately. A lack of contraction following that stimulation would therefore suggest damage at those levels.

card.q: The location of somatosensation is based on the topographical map of sensory innervation. What does this mean?
card.a: Where spinal nerves innervate the skin is represented by “slices” of the body surface referred to as dermatomes. The fibers originating in each region are contained within the same spinal nerve, which relates to the perception of that localization.

card.q: Why are upper motor neuron lesions characterized by “spastic paralysis”?
card.a: Paralysis means that voluntary muscle control is not possible because of the interruption of descending motor input. Spasticity refers to what could be called “hypercontractility” of the muscles in the absence of the descending input.

q: Which white matter structure carries information from the cerebral cortex to the cerebellum?
why: The correct answer is: middle cerebellar peduncle. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which region of the cerebellum receives proprioceptive input from the spinal cord?
why: The correct answer is: vermis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following tests cerebellar function related to gait?
why: The correct answer is: station. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is not a cause of cerebellar ataxia?
why: The correct answer is: antibiotics. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following functions cannot be attributed to the cerebellum?
options: comparing motor commands and sensory feedback
associating sensory stimuli with learned behavior
why: The correct answer is: processing visual information. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Learning to ride a bike is a motor function dependent on the cerebellum. Why are the different regions of the cerebellum involved in this complex motor learning?
card.a: The spinocerebellum is related to controlling the axial muscles and keeps the body balanced on the bike. The cerebrocerebellum is related to controlling the appendicular muscles and keeps the legs moving to pedal the bike. The vestibulocerebellum receives input about equilibrium to help keep everything balanced as the bike is moving forward.

card.q: Alcohol intoxication can produce slurred speech. How is this related to cerebellar function?
card.a: Rapid alternating movements in speech relate to how the lips, tongue, and palate move to produce speech sounds. The cerebrocerebellum is required for the proper implementation of these movements.

q: Endocrine glands ________.
options: secrete hormones that travel through a duct to the target organs
release neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft
secrete chemical messengers that travel in the bloodstream
include sebaceous glands and sweat glands
why: The correct answer is: secrete chemical messengers that travel in the bloodstream. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Chemical signaling that affects neighboring cells is called ________.
why: The correct answer is: paracrine. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “chemical signal that elicits a response in the same cell that secreted it”
why: autocrine: chemical signal that elicits a response in the same cell that secreted it

q: Which term matches this definition? “tissue or organ that secretes hormones into the blood and lymph without ducts such that they may be transported to organs distant from the site of secretion”
why: endocrine gland: tissue or organ that secretes hormones into the blood and lymph without ducts such that they may be transported to organs distant from the site of secretion

q: Which term matches this definition? “cells, tissues, and organs that secrete hormones as a primary or secondary function and play an integral role in normal bodily processes”
why: endocrine system: cells, tissues, and organs that secrete hormones as a primary or secondary function and play an integral role in normal bodily processes

q: Which term matches this definition? “cells, tissues, and organs that secrete substances directly to target tissues via glandular ducts”
why: exocrine system: cells, tissues, and organs that secrete substances directly to target tissues via glandular ducts

q: Which term matches this definition? “secretion of an endocrine organ that travels via the bloodstream or lymphatics to induce a response in target cells or tissues in another part of the body”
why: hormone: secretion of an endocrine organ that travels via the bloodstream or lymphatics to induce a response in target cells or tissues in another part of the body

q: Which term matches this definition? “chemical signal that elicits a response in neighboring cells; also called paracrine factor”
why: paracrine: chemical signal that elicits a response in neighboring cells; also called paracrine factor

card.q: Describe several main differences in the communication methods used by the endocrine system and the nervous system.
card.a: The endocrine system uses chemical signals called hormones to convey information from one part of the body to a distant part of the body. Hormones are released from the endocrine cell into the extracellular environment, but then travel in the bloodstream to target tissues. This communication and response can take seconds to days. In contrast, neurons transmit electrical signals along their axons. At the axon terminal, the electrical signal prompts the release of a chemical signal called a neurotransmitter that carries the message across the synaptic cleft to elicit a response in the neighboring cell. This method of communication is nearly instantaneous, of very brief duration, and is highly specific.

card.q: Compare and contrast endocrine and exocrine glands.
card.a: Endocrine glands are ductless. They release their secretion into the surrounding fluid, from which it enters the bloodstream or lymph to travel to distant cells. Moreover, the secretions of endocrine glands are hormones. Exocrine glands release their secretions through a duct that delivers the secretion to the target location. Moreover, the secretions of exocrine glands are not hormones, but compounds that have an immediate physiologic function. For example, pancreatic juice contains enzymes that help digest food.

card.q: True or false: Neurotransmitters are a special class of paracrines. Explain your answer.
card.a: True. Neurotransmitters can be classified as paracrines because, upon their release from a neuron’s axon terminals, they travel across a microscopically small cleft to exert their effect on a nearby neuron or muscle cell.

q: A newly developed pesticide has been observed to bind to an intracellular hormone receptor. If ingested, residue from this pesticide could disrupt levels of ________.
why: The correct answer is: thyroid hormone. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A small molecule binds to a G protein, preventing its activation. What direct effect will this have on signaling that involves cAMP?
options: The hormone will not be able to bind to the hormone receptor.
Adenylyl cyclase will not be activated.
Excessive quantities of cAMP will be produced.
The phosphorylation cascade will be initiated.
why: The correct answer is: Adenylyl cyclase will not be activated.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A student is in a car accident, and although not hurt, immediately experiences pupil dilation, increased heart rate, and rapid breathing. What type of endocrine system stimulus did the student receive?
why: The correct answer is: neural. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “membrane-bound enzyme that converts ATP to cyclic AMP, creating cAMP, as a result of G-protein activation”
why: adenylyl cyclase: membrane-bound enzyme that converts ATP to cyclic AMP, creating cAMP, as a result of G-protein activation

q: Which term matches this definition? “second messenger that, in response to adenylyl cyclase activation, triggers a phosphorylation cascade”
why: cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP): second messenger that, in response to adenylyl cyclase activation, triggers a phosphorylation cascade

q: Which term matches this definition? “molecule that, like cAMP, activates protein kinases, thereby initiating a phosphorylation cascade”
why: diacylglycerol (DAG): molecule that, like cAMP, activates protein kinases, thereby initiating a phosphorylation cascade

q: Which term matches this definition? “decrease in the number of hormone receptors, typically in response to chronically excessive levels of a hormone”
why: downregulation: decrease in the number of hormone receptors, typically in response to chronically excessive levels of a hormone

q: Which term matches this definition? “hormone that binds to a cell membrane hormone receptor and triggers activation of a second messenger system”
why: first messenger: hormone that binds to a cell membrane hormone receptor and triggers activation of a second messenger system

q: Which term matches this definition? “protein associated with a cell membrane hormone receptor that initiates the next step in a second messenger system upon activation by hormone–receptor binding”
why: G protein: protein associated with a cell membrane hormone receptor that initiates the next step in a second messenger system upon activation by hormone–receptor binding

card.q: Compare and contrast the signaling events involved with the second messengers cAMP and IP₃.
card.a: In both cAMP and IP₃–calcium signaling, a hormone binds to a cell membrane hormone receptor that is coupled to a G protein. The G protein becomes activated when the hormone binds. In the case of cAMP signaling, the activated G protein activates adenylyl cyclase, which causes ATP to be converted to cAMP. This second messenger can then initiate other signaling events, such as a phosphorylation cascade. In the case of IP₃–calcium signaling, the activated G protein activates phospholipase C, which cleaves a membrane phospholipid compound into DAG and IP₃. IP₃ causes the release of calcium, another second messenger, from intracellular stores. This causes further signaling events.

card.q: Describe the mechanism of hormone response resulting from the binding of a hormone with an intracellular receptor.
card.a: An intracellular hormone receptor is located within the cell. A hydrophobic hormone diffuses through the cell membrane and binds to the intracellular hormone receptor, which may be in the cytosol or in the cell nucleus. This hormone–receptor complex binds to a segment of DNA. This initiates the transcription of a target gene, the end result of which is protein assembly and the hormonal response.

q: The hypothalamus is functionally and anatomically connected to the posterior pituitary lobe by a bridge of ________.
why: The correct answer is: nerve axons. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is an anterior pituitary hormone?
why: The correct answer is: TSH. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: How many hormones are produced by the posterior pituitary?
why: The correct answer is: 0. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following hormones contributes to the regulation of the body’s fluid and electrolyte balance?
why: The correct answer is: antidiuretic hormone. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “disorder in adults caused when abnormally high levels of GH trigger growth of bones in the face, hands, and feet”
why: acromegaly: disorder in adults caused when abnormally high levels of GH trigger growth of bones in the face, hands, and feet

q: Which term matches this definition? “anterior pituitary hormone that stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete corticosteroid hormones (also called corticotropin)”
why: adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH): anterior pituitary hormone that stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete corticosteroid hormones (also called corticotropin)

q: Which term matches this definition? “hypothalamic hormone that is stored by the posterior pituitary and that signals the kidneys to reabsorb water”
why: antidiuretic hormone (ADH): hypothalamic hormone that is stored by the posterior pituitary and that signals the kidneys to reabsorb water

q: Which term matches this definition? “anterior pituitary hormone that stimulates the production and maturation of sex cells”
why: follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH): anterior pituitary hormone that stimulates the production and maturation of sex cells

q: Which term matches this definition? “disorder in children caused when abnormally high levels of GH prompt excessive growth”
why: gigantism: disorder in children caused when abnormally high levels of GH prompt excessive growth

q: Which term matches this definition? “hormones that regulate the function of the gonads”
why: gonadotropins: hormones that regulate the function of the gonads

card.q: Visit this link to watch an animation showing the role of the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland. Which hormone is released by the pituitary to stimulate the thyroid gland?
card.a: Thyroid-stimulating hormone.

card.q: Compare and contrast the anatomical relationship of the anterior and posterior lobes of the pituitary gland to the hypothalamus.
card.a: The anterior lobe of the pituitary gland is connected to the hypothalamus by vasculature, which allows regulating hormones from the hypothalamus to travel to the anterior pituitary. In contrast, the posterior lobe is connected to the hypothalamus by a bridge of nerve axons called the hypothalamic–hypophyseal tract, along which the hypothalamus sends hormones produced by hypothalamic nerve cell bodies to the posterior pituitary for storage and release into the circulation.

card.q: Name the target tissues for prolactin.
card.a: The mammary glands are the target tissues for prolactin.

q: Which of the following statements about the thyroid gland is true?
options: It is located anterior to the trachea and inferior to the larynx.
The parathyroid glands are embedded within it.
why: The correct answer is: all of the above. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The secretion of thyroid hormones is controlled by ________.
options: thyroglobulin from the thyroid’s parafollicular cells
why: The correct answer is: TSH from the anterior pituitary. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The development of a goiter indicates that ________.
options: the anterior pituitary is abnormally enlarged
there is hypertrophy of the thyroid’s follicle cells
there is an excessive accumulation of colloid in the thyroid follicles
the anterior pituitary is secreting excessive growth hormone
why: The correct answer is: there is an excessive accumulation of colloid in the thyroid follicles. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Iodide ions cross from the bloodstream into follicle cells via ________.
why: The correct answer is: active transport. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “peptide hormone produced and secreted by the parafollicular cells (C cells) of the thyroid gland that functions to decrease blood calcium levels”
why: calcitonin: peptide hormone produced and secreted by the parafollicular cells (C cells) of the thyroid gland that functions to decrease blood calcium levels

q: Which term matches this definition? “viscous fluid in the central cavity of thyroid follicles, containing the glycoprotein thyroglobulin”
why: colloid: viscous fluid in the central cavity of thyroid follicles, containing the glycoprotein thyroglobulin

q: Which term matches this definition? “enlargement of the thyroid gland either as a result of iodine deficiency or hyperthyroidism”
why: goiter: enlargement of the thyroid gland either as a result of iodine deficiency or hyperthyroidism

q: Which term matches this definition? “clinically abnormal, elevated level of thyroid hormone in the blood; characterized by an increased metabolic rate, excess body heat, sweating, diarrhea, weight loss, and increased heart rate”
why: hyperthyroidism: clinically abnormal, elevated level of thyroid hormone in the blood; characterized by an increased metabolic rate, excess body heat, sweating, diarrhea, weight loss, and increased heart rate

q: Which term matches this definition? “clinically abnormal, low level of thyroid hormone in the blood; characterized by low metabolic rate, weight gain, cold extremities, constipation, and reduced mental activity”
why: hypothyroidism: clinically abnormal, low level of thyroid hormone in the blood; characterized by low metabolic rate, weight gain, cold extremities, constipation, and reduced mental activity

q: Which term matches this definition? “condition characterized by cognitive deficits, short stature, and other signs and symptoms in people born to people who were iodine-deficient during pregnancy”
why: neonatal hypothyroidism: condition characterized by cognitive deficits, short stature, and other signs and symptoms in people born to people who were iodine-deficient during pregnancy

card.q: Explain why maternal iodine deficiency might lead to neurological impairment in the fetus.
card.a: Iodine deficiency in a pregnant woman would also deprive the fetus. Iodine is required for the synthesis of thyroid hormones, which contribute to fetal growth and development, including maturation of the nervous system. Insufficient amounts would impair these functions.

card.q: Define hyperthyroidism and explain why one of its symptoms is weight loss.
card.a: Hyperthyroidism is an abnormally elevated blood level of thyroid hormones due to an overproduction of T₃ and T₄. An individual with hyperthyroidism is likely to lose weight because one of the primary roles of thyroid hormones is to increase the body’s basal metabolic rate, increasing the breakdown of nutrients and the production of ATP.

q: When blood calcium levels are low, PTH stimulates ________.
options: urinary excretion of calcium by the kidneys
a reduction in calcium absorption from the intestines
why: The correct answer is: the activity of osteoclasts. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following can result from hyperparathyroidism?
why: The correct answer is: fractures. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “disorder caused by overproduction of PTH that results in abnormally elevated blood calcium”
why: hyperparathyroidism: disorder caused by overproduction of PTH that results in abnormally elevated blood calcium

q: Which term matches this definition? “disorder caused by underproduction of PTH that results in abnormally low blood calcium”
why: hypoparathyroidism: disorder caused by underproduction of PTH that results in abnormally low blood calcium

q: Which term matches this definition? “small, round glands embedded in the posterior thyroid gland that produce parathyroid hormone (PTH)”
why: parathyroid glands: small, round glands embedded in the posterior thyroid gland that produce parathyroid hormone (PTH)

q: Which term matches this definition? “peptide hormone produced and secreted by the parathyroid glands in response to low blood calcium levels”
why: parathyroid hormone (PTH): peptide hormone produced and secreted by the parathyroid glands in response to low blood calcium levels

card.q: Describe the role of negative feedback in the function of the parathyroid gland.
card.a: The production and secretion of PTH is regulated by a negative feedback loop. Low blood calcium levels initiate the production and secretion of PTH. PTH increases bone resorption, calcium absorption from the intestines, and calcium reabsorption by the kidneys. As a result, blood calcium levels begin to rise. This, in turn, inhibits the further production and secretion of PTH.

card.q: Explain why someone with a parathyroid gland tumor might develop kidney stones.
card.a: A parathyroid gland tumor can prompt hypersecretion of PTH. This can raise blood calcium levels so excessively that calcium deposits begin to accumulate throughout the body, including in the kidney tubules, where they are referred to as kidney stones.

q: The adrenal glands are attached superiorly to which organ?
why: The correct answer is: kidneys. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What secretory cell type is found in the adrenal medulla?
why: The correct answer is: chromaffin cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Cushing’s disease is a disorder caused by ________.
why: The correct answer is: abnormally high levels of cortisol. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following responses is not part of the fight-or-flight response?
options: increased oxygen supply to the lungs
why: The correct answer is: reduced mental activity. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “outer region of the adrenal glands consisting of multiple layers of epithelial cells and capillary networks that produces mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids”
why: adrenal cortex: outer region of the adrenal glands consisting of multiple layers of epithelial cells and capillary networks that produces mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids

q: Which term matches this definition? “endocrine glands located at the top of each kidney that are important for the regulation of the stress response, blood pressure and blood volume, water homeostasis, and electrolyte levels”
why: adrenal glands: endocrine glands located at the top of each kidney that are important for the regulation of the stress response, blood pressure and blood volume, water homeostasis, and electrolyte levels

q: Which term matches this definition? “inner layer of the adrenal glands that plays an important role in the stress response by producing epinephrine and norepinephrine”
why: adrenal medulla: inner layer of the adrenal glands that plays an important role in the stress response by producing epinephrine and norepinephrine

q: Which term matches this definition? “the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II”
why: angiotensin-converting enzyme: the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II

q: Which term matches this definition? “the short-term stress, or the fight-or-flight response, of stage one of the general adaptation syndrome mediated by the hormones epinephrine and norepinephrine”
why: alarm reaction: the short-term stress, or the fight-or-flight response, of stage one of the general adaptation syndrome mediated by the hormones epinephrine and norepinephrine

q: Which term matches this definition? “hormone produced and secreted by the adrenal cortex that stimulates sodium and fluid retention and increases blood volume and blood pressure”
why: aldosterone: hormone produced and secreted by the adrenal cortex that stimulates sodium and fluid retention and increases blood volume and blood pressure

card.q: Visit this link to view an animation describing the location and function of the adrenal glands. Which hormone produced by the adrenal glands is responsible for mobilization of energy stores?
card.a: Cortisol.

card.q: What are the three regions of the adrenal cortex and what hormones do they produce?
card.a: The outer region is the zona glomerulosa, which produces mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone; the next region is the zona fasciculata, which produces glucocorticoids such as cortisol; the inner region is the zona reticularis, which produces androgens.

card.q: If innervation to the adrenal medulla were disrupted, what would be the physiological outcome?
card.a: Damage to the innervation of the adrenal medulla would prevent the adrenal glands from responding to the hypothalamus during the fight-or-flight response. Therefore, the response would be reduced.

card.q: Compare and contrast the short-term and long-term stress response.
card.a: The short-term stress response involves the hormones epinephrine and norepinephrine, which work to increase the oxygen supply to organs important for extreme muscular action such as the brain, lungs, and muscles. In the long-term stress response, the hormone cortisol is involved in catabolism of glycogen stores, proteins, and triglycerides, glucose and ketone synthesis, and downregulation of the immune system.

q: What cells secrete melatonin?
why: The correct answer is: pinealocytes. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The production of melatonin is inhibited by ________.
why: The correct answer is: exposure to bright light. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “amino acid–derived hormone that is secreted in response to low light and causes drowsiness”
why: melatonin: amino acid–derived hormone that is secreted in response to low light and causes drowsiness

q: Which term matches this definition? “endocrine gland that secretes melatonin, which is important in regulating the sleep-wake cycle”
why: pineal gland: endocrine gland that secretes melatonin, which is important in regulating the sleep-wake cycle

q: Which term matches this definition? “cell of the pineal gland that produces and secretes the hormone melatonin”
why: pinealocyte: cell of the pineal gland that produces and secretes the hormone melatonin

card.q: Visit this link to view a presentation describing the function of the hormone melatonin. What should you avoid doing in the middle of your sleep cycle that would lower melatonin?
card.a: Turning on the lights.

card.q: Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) is a mood disorder characterized by, among other symptoms, increased appetite, sluggishness, and increased sleepiness. It occurs most commonly during the winter months, especially in regions with long winter nights. Propose a role for melatonin in SAD and a possible non-drug therapy.
card.a: SAD is thought to occur in part because low levels and duration of sunlight allow excessive and prolonged secretion of melatonin. Light therapy—daytime exposure to very bright lighting—is one common therapy.

card.q: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a disease that causes deterioration of the retinas of the eyes. Describe the impact RP would have on melatonin levels.
card.a: The retina is important for melatonin production because it senses light. Bright light inhibits the production of melatonin, whereas low light levels promote the production of melatonin. Therefore, deterioration of the retinas would most likely disturb the sleep-wake pattern because melatonin production would be elevated.

q: The gonads produce what class of hormones?
why: The correct answer is: steroid hormones. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The production of FSH by the anterior pituitary is reduced by which hormone?
why: The correct answer is: inhibin. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The function of the placental hormone human placental lactogen (hPL) is to ________.
why: The correct answer is: prepare the breasts for lactation. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “class of predominantly female sex hormones important for the development and growth of the female reproductive tract, secondary sex characteristics, the female reproductive cycle, and the maintenance of pregnancy”
why: estrogens: class of predominantly female sex hormones important for the development and growth of the female reproductive tract, secondary sex characteristics, the female reproductive cycle, and the maintenance of pregnancy

q: Which term matches this definition? “hormone secreted by the male and female gonads that inhibits FSH production by the anterior pituitary”
why: inhibin: hormone secreted by the male and female gonads that inhibits FSH production by the anterior pituitary

q: Which term matches this definition? “predominantly female sex hormone important in regulating the female reproductive cycle and the maintenance of pregnancy”
why: progesterone: predominantly female sex hormone important in regulating the female reproductive cycle and the maintenance of pregnancy

q: Which term matches this definition? “steroid hormone secreted by the testes and important in the maturation of sperm cells, growth and development of the reproductive system, and the development of secondary sex characteristics”
why: testosterone: steroid hormone secreted by the testes and important in the maturation of sperm cells, growth and development of the reproductive system, and the development of secondary sex characteristics

card.q: Compare and contrast the role of estrogens and progesterone.
card.a: Both estrogens and progesterone are steroid hormones produced by the ovaries that help regulate the menstrual cycle. Estrogens play an important role in the development of the female reproductive tract and secondary sex characteristics. They also help maintain pregnancy. Progesterone prepares the body for pregnancy and helps maintain pregnancy.

card.q: Describe the role of placental secretion of relaxin in preparation for childbirth.
card.a: Relaxin produced by the placenta is thought to soften and widen the pubic symphysis. This increases the size of the pelvic outlet, the birth canal through which the fetus passes during vaginal childbirth.

q: If an autoimmune disorder targets the alpha cells, production of which hormone would be directly affected?
why: The correct answer is: glucagon. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following statements about insulin is true?
options: Insulin acts as a transport protein, carrying glucose across the cell membrane.
Insulin facilitates the movement of intracellular glucose transporters to the cell membrane.
Insulin stimulates the breakdown of stored glycogen into glucose.
Insulin stimulates the kidneys to reabsorb glucose into the bloodstream.
why: The correct answer is: Insulin facilitates the movement of intracellular glucose transporters to the cell membrane.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “pancreatic islet cell type that produces the hormone glucagon”
why: alpha cell: pancreatic islet cell type that produces the hormone glucagon

q: Which term matches this definition? “pancreatic islet cell type that produces the hormone insulin”
why: beta cell: pancreatic islet cell type that produces the hormone insulin

q: Which term matches this definition? “minor cell type in the pancreas that secretes the hormone somatostatin”
why: delta cell: minor cell type in the pancreas that secretes the hormone somatostatin

q: Which term matches this definition? “condition caused by destruction or dysfunction of the beta cells of the pancreas or cellular resistance to insulin that results in abnormally high blood glucose levels”
why: diabetes mellitus: condition caused by destruction or dysfunction of the beta cells of the pancreas or cellular resistance to insulin that results in abnormally high blood glucose levels

q: Which term matches this definition? “pancreatic hormone that stimulates the catabolism of glycogen to glucose, thereby increasing blood glucose levels”
why: glucagon: pancreatic hormone that stimulates the catabolism of glycogen to glucose, thereby increasing blood glucose levels

q: Which term matches this definition? “abnormally high blood glucose levels”
why: hyperglycemia: abnormally high blood glucose levels

card.q: Visit this link to view an animation describing the location and function of the pancreas. What goes wrong in the function of insulin in type 2 diabetes?
card.a: Insulin is overproduced.

card.q: What would be the physiological consequence of a disease that destroyed the beta cells of the pancreas?
card.a: The beta cells produce the hormone insulin, which is important in the regulation of blood glucose levels. All insulin-dependent cells of the body require insulin in order to take up glucose from the bloodstream. Destruction of the beta cells would result in an inability to produce and secrete insulin, leading to abnormally high blood glucose levels and the disease called type 1 diabetes mellitus.

card.q: Why is foot care extremely important for people with diabetes mellitus?
card.a: Excessive blood glucose levels damage the blood vessels and nerves of the body’s extremities, increasing the risk for injury, infection, and tissue death. Loss of sensation to the feet means that a diabetic patient will not be able to feel foot trauma, such as from ill-fitting shoes. Even minor injuries commonly lead to infection, which, can progress to tissue death without proper care, requiring amputation.

q: The walls of the atria produce which hormone?
why: The correct answer is: atrial natriuretic peptide. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The end result of the RAAS is to ________.
why: The correct answer is: increase blood pressure. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Athletes may take synthetic EPO to boost their ________.
why: The correct answer is: blood oxygen levels. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Hormones produced by the thymus play a role in the ________.
options: preparation of the body for childbirth
release of hydrochloric acid in the stomach
why: The correct answer is: development of T cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “peptide hormone produced by the walls of the atria in response to high blood pressure, blood volume, or blood sodium that reduces the reabsorption of sodium and water in the kidneys and promotes vasodilation”
why: atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP): peptide hormone produced by the walls of the atria in response to high blood pressure, blood volume, or blood sodium that reduces the reabsorption of sodium and water in the kidneys and promotes vasodilation

q: Which term matches this definition? “protein hormone secreted in response to low oxygen levels that triggers the bone marrow to produce red blood cells”
why: erythropoietin (EPO): protein hormone secreted in response to low oxygen levels that triggers the bone marrow to produce red blood cells

q: Which term matches this definition? “protein hormone secreted by adipose tissues in response to food consumption that promotes satiety”
why: leptin: protein hormone secreted by adipose tissues in response to food consumption that promotes satiety

q: Which term matches this definition? “hormones produced and secreted by the thymus that play an important role in the development and differentiation of T cells”
why: thymosins: hormones produced and secreted by the thymus that play an important role in the development and differentiation of T cells

q: Which term matches this definition? “organ that is involved in the development and maturation of T-cells and is particularly active during infancy and childhood”
why: thymus: organ that is involved in the development and maturation of T-cells and is particularly active during infancy and childhood

card.q: Summarize the role of GI tract hormones following a meal.
card.a: The presence of food in the GI tract stimulates the release of hormones that aid in digestion. For example, gastrin is secreted in response to stomach distention and causes the release of hydrochloric acid in the stomach. Secretin is secreted when acidic chyme enters the small intestine, and stimulates the release of pancreatic bicarbonate. In the presence of fat and protein in the duodenum, CCK stimulates the release of pancreatic digestive enzymes and bile from the gallbladder. Other GI tract hormones aid in glucose metabolism and other functions.

card.q: Compare and contrast the thymus gland in infancy and adulthood.
card.a: The thymus gland is important for the development and maturation of T cells. During infancy and early childhood, the thymus gland is large and very active, as the immune system is still developing. During adulthood, the thymus gland atrophies because the immune system is already developed.

q: The anterior pituitary gland develops from which embryonic germ layer?
why: The correct answer is: oral ectoderm. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: In the elderly, decreased thyroid function causes ________.
why: The correct answer is: decreased basal metabolic rate. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Distinguish between the effects of menopause and andropause on fertility.
card.a: Menopause occurs as the result of a progressive decline in the function of the ovaries, resulting in low estrogen and progesterone levels. Ovulation ceases, and postmenopausal woman can no longer conceive a child. In contrast, andropause is a much more gradual and subtle decline in testosterone levels and functioning. A man typically maintains fertility until very old age, although the quantity, quality, and motility of the sperm he produces may be reduced.

q: Which of the following statements about blood is true?

Blood is slightly more salty than seawater.

It is the most abundant plasma protein.

card.q: Visit this site for a list of normal levels established for many of the substances found in a sample of blood. card.q: A patient’s hematocrit is 42 percent. Approximately what percentage of the patient’s blood is plasma?
card.a: The patient’s blood is approximately 58 percent plasma (since the buffy coat is less than 1 percent).

card.q: Why would it be incorrect to refer to the formed elements as cells?
card.a: The formed elements include erythrocytes and leukocytes, which are cells (although mature erythrocytes do not have a nucleus); however, the formed elements also include platelets, which are not true cells but cell fragments.

card.q: True or false: The buffy coat is the portion of a blood sample that is made up of its proteins.
card.a: False. The buffy coat is the portion of blood that is made up of its leukocytes and platelets.

q: Which of the formed elements arise from myeloid stem cells?

card.q: Watch this video to see doctors discuss the dangers of blood doping in sports. What are the some potential side effects of blood doping?

card.q: Myelofibrosis is a disorder in which inflammation and scar tissue formation in the bone marrow impair hemopoiesis. One sign is an enlarged spleen. Why?
card.a: When disease impairs the ability of the bone marrow to participate in hemopoiesis, extramedullary hemopoiesis begins in the patient’s liver and spleen. This causes the spleen to enlarge.

card.q: Would you expect a patient with a form of cancer called acute myelogenous leukemia to experience impaired production of erythrocytes, or impaired production of lymphocytes? Explain your choice.
card.a: The adjective myelogenous suggests a condition originating from (generated by) myeloid cells. Acute myelogenous leukemia impairs the production of erythrocytes and other mature formed elements of the myeloid stem cell lineage. Lymphocytes arise from the lymphoid stem cell line.

q: Which of the following statements about mature, circulating erythrocytes is true?

contains four glycoprotein units studded with oxygen
consists of four globin proteins, each bound to a molecule of heme
can carry up to 120 molecules of oxygen

q: The production of healthy erythrocytes depends upon the availability of ________.

q: Aging and damaged erythrocytes are removed from the circulation by ________.

q: A patient has been suffering for 2 months with a chronic, watery diarrhea. A blood test is likely to reveal ________.
why: The correct answer is: polycythemia. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: A young person has been experiencing unusually heavy menstrual bleeding for several years. They follow a strict vegan diet (no animal foods). They are is at risk for what disorder, and why?
card.a: They are at risk for anemia, because their unusually heavy menstrual bleeding results in excessive loss of erythrocytes each month. At the same time, their vegan diet means that they do not have dietary sources of heme iron. The non-heme iron they consume in plant foods is not as well absorbed as heme iron.

card.q: A patient has thalassemia, a genetic disorder characterized by abnormal synthesis of globin proteins and excessive destruction of erythrocytes. This patient is jaundiced and is found to have an excessive level of bilirubin in their blood. Explain the connection.
card.a: Bilirubin is a breakdown product of the non-iron component of heme, which is cleaved from globin when erythrocytes are degraded. Excessive erythrocyte destruction would deposit excessive bilirubin in the blood. Bilirubin is a yellowish pigment, and high blood levels can manifest as yellowed skin.

q: The process by which leukocytes squeeze through adjacent cells in a blood vessel wall is called ________.
why: The correct answer is: emigration. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following describes a neutrophil?

abundant, granular, especially effective against bacteria
rare, granular, contains multiple granules packed with histamine

q: T and B lymphocytes ________.

are most active against parasitic worms

q: A patient has been experiencing severe, persistent allergy symptoms that are reduced when she takes an antihistamine. Before the treatment, this patient was likely to have had increased activity of which leukocyte?
why: The correct answer is: basophils. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Thrombocytes are more accurately called ________.
why: The correct answer is: platelets. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: One of the more common adverse effects of cancer chemotherapy is the destruction of leukocytes. Before his next scheduled chemotherapy treatment, a patient undergoes a blood test called an absolute neutrophil count (ANC), which reveals that his neutrophil count is 1900 cells per microliter. Would his healthcare team be likely to proceed with his chemotherapy treatment? Why?
card.a: A neutrophil count below 1800 cells per microliter is considered abnormal. Thus, this patient’s ANC is at the low end of the normal range and there would be no reason to delay chemotherapy. In clinical practice, most patients are given chemotherapy if their ANC is above 1000.

card.q: A patient was admitted to the burn unit the previous evening suffering from a severe burn involving their left upper extremity and shoulder. A blood test reveals that they are experiencing leukocytosis. Why is this an expected finding?
card.a: Any severe stress can increase the leukocyte count, resulting in leukocytosis. A burn is especially likely to increase the proliferation of leukocytes in order to ward off infection, a significant risk when the barrier function of the skin is destroyed.

q: The first step in hemostasis is ________.
why: The correct answer is: vascular spasm. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Prothrombin is converted to thrombin during the ________.

q: Which term matches this definition? “thrombus that has broken free from the blood vessel wall and entered the circulation”

card.q: View these animations to explore the intrinsic, extrinsic, and common pathways that are involved the process of coagulation. The coagulation cascade restores hemostasis by activating coagulation factors in the presence of an injury.
card.a: Clotting factors flow through the blood vessels in their inactive state. The endothelium does not have thrombogenic tissue factor to activate clotting factors.

card.q: A lab technician collects a blood sample in a glass tube. After about an hour, she harvests serum to continue her blood analysis. Explain what has happened during the hour that the sample was in the glass tube.
card.a: When blood contacts glass, the intrinsic coagulation pathway is initiated. This leads to the common pathway, and the blood clots. Within about 30 minutes, the clot begins to shrink. After an hour, it is about half its original size. Its heavier weight will cause it to fall to the bottom of the tube during centrifugation, allowing the lab technician to harvest the serum remaining at the top.

card.q: Explain why administration of a thrombolytic agent is a first intervention for someone who has suffered a thrombotic stroke.
card.a: In a thrombotic stroke, a blood vessel to the brain has been blocked by a thrombus, an aggregation of platelets and erythrocytes within a blood vessel. A thrombolytic agent is a medication that promotes the breakup of thrombi.

q: The process in which antibodies attach to antigens, causing the formation of masses of linked cells, is called ________.
why: The correct answer is: agglutination. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: People with ABO blood type O ________.

lack both antigens A and B on their erythrocytes
have neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies circulating in their blood plasma

a type O person is carrying a type AB fetus
an Rh⁺ person is carrying an Rh⁻ fetus

card.q: Following a motor vehicle accident, a patient is rushed to the emergency department with multiple traumatic injuries, causing severe bleeding. The patient’s condition is critical, and there is no time for determining their blood type. What type of blood is transfused, and why?
card.a: In emergency situations, blood type O⁻ will be infused until cross matching can be done. Blood type O⁻ is called the universal donor blood because the erythrocytes have neither A nor B antigens on their surface, and the Rh factor is negative.

card.q: In preparation for a scheduled surgery, a patient visits the hospital lab for a blood draw. The technician collects a blood sample and performs a test to determine its type. She places a sample of the patient’s blood in two wells. To the first well she adds anti-A antibody. To the second she adds anti-B antibody. Both samples visibly agglutinate. Has the technician made an error, or is this a normal response? If normal, what blood type does this indicate?
card.a: The lab technician has not made an error. Blood type AB has both A and B surface antigens, and neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies circulating in the plasma. When anti-A antibodies (added to the first well) contact A antigens on AB erythrocytes, they will cause agglutination. Similarly, when anti-B antibodies contact B antigens on AB erythrocytes, they will cause agglutination.

q: Which of the following is not important in preventing backflow of blood?
why: The correct answer is: endocardium. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which valve separates the left atrium from the left ventricle?

q: Which of the following lists the valves in the order through which the blood flows from the vena cava through the heart?

aortic semilunar, pulmonary semilunar, tricuspid, bicuspid
bicuspid, aortic semilunar, tricuspid, pulmonary semilunar
why: The correct answer is: tricuspid, pulmonary semilunar, bicuspid, aortic semilunar. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which chamber initially receives blood from the systemic circuit?
why: The correct answer is: right atrium. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The ________ layer secretes chemicals that help to regulate ionic environments and strength of contraction and serve as powerful vasoconstrictors.
why: The correct answer is: endocardium. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The myocardium would be the thickest in the ________.
why: The correct answer is: left ventricle. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: In which septum is it normal to find openings in the adult?
why: The correct answer is: atrioventricular septum. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Visit this site to observe an echocardiogram of actual heart valves opening and closing. Although much of the heart has been “removed” from this gif loop so the chordae tendineae are not visible, why is their presence more critical for the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and mitral) than the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves?
card.a: The pressure gradient between the atria and the ventricles is much greater than that between the ventricles and the pulmonary trunk and aorta. Without the presence of the chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, the valves would be blown back (prolapsed) into the atria and blood would regurgitate.

card.q: Describe how the valves keep the blood moving in one direction.
card.a: When the ventricles contract and pressure begins to rise in the ventricles, there is an initial tendency for blood to flow back (regurgitate) to the atria. However, the papillary muscles also contract, placing tension on the chordae tendineae and holding the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and mitral) in place to prevent the valves from prolapsing and being forced back into the atria. The semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) lack chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, but do not face the same pressure gradients as do the atrioventricular valves. As the ventricles relax and pressure drops within the ventricles, there is a tendency for the blood to flow backward. However, the valves, consisting of reinforced endothelium and connective tissue, fill with blood and seal off the opening preventing the return of blood.

card.q: Why is the pressure in the pulmonary circulation lower than in the systemic circulation?
card.a: The pulmonary circuit consists of blood flowing to and from the lungs, whereas the systemic circuit carries blood to and from the entire body. The systemic circuit is far more extensive, consisting of far more vessels and offers much greater resistance to the flow of blood, so the heart must generate a higher pressure to overcome this resistance. This can be seen in the thickness of the myocardium in the ventricles.

q: Which component of the heart conduction system would have the slowest rate of firing?

q: Which term matches this definition? “(also, interatrial band) group of specialized conducting cells that transmit the impulse directly from the SA node in the right atrium to the left atrium”
why: Bachmann’s bundle: (also, interatrial band) group of specialized conducting cells that transmit the impulse directly from the SA node in the right atrium to the left atrium

q: Which term matches this definition? “(also, atrioventricular bundle) group of specialized myocardial conductile cells that transmit the impulse from the AV node through the interventricular septum; form the left and right atrioventricular bundle branches”
why: bundle of His: (also, atrioventricular bundle) group of specialized myocardial conductile cells that transmit the impulse from the AV node through the interventricular septum; form the left and right atrioventricular bundle branches

q: Which term matches this definition? “surface recording of the electrical activity of the heart that can be used for diagnosis of irregular heart function; also abbreviated as EKG”
why: electrocardiogram (ECG): surface recording of the electrical activity of the heart that can be used for diagnosis of irregular heart function; also abbreviated as EKG

card.q: Why is the plateau phase so critical to cardiac muscle function?
card.a: It prevents additional impulses from spreading through the heart prematurely, thereby allowing the muscle sufficient time to contract and pump blood effectively.

card.q: How does the delay of the impulse at the atrioventricular node contribute to cardiac function?
card.a: It ensures sufficient time for the atrial muscle to contract and pump blood into the ventricles prior to the impulse being conducted into the lower chambers.

card.q: How do gap junctions and intercalated disks aid contraction of the heart?
card.a: Gap junctions within the intercalated disks allow impulses to spread from one cardiac muscle cell to another, allowing sodium, potassium, and calcium ions to flow between adjacent cells, propagating the action potential, and ensuring coordinated contractions.

card.q: Why do the cardiac muscles cells demonstrate autorhythmicity?
card.a: Without a true resting potential, there is a slow influx of sodium ions through slow channels that produces a prepotential that gradually reaches threshold.

q: The cardiac cycle consists of a distinct relaxation and contraction phase. Which term is typically used to refer ventricular contraction while no blood is being ejected?
why: The correct answer is: isovolumic contraction. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Most blood enters the ventricle during ________.
why: The correct answer is: atrial diastole. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The first heart sound represents which portion of the cardiac cycle?
why: The correct answer is: closing of the atrioventricular valves. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Ventricular relaxation immediately follows ________.
why: The correct answer is: ventricular repolarization. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “period of time between the onset of atrial contraction (atrial systole) and ventricular relaxation (ventricular diastole)”
why: cardiac cycle: period of time between the onset of atrial contraction (atrial systole) and ventricular relaxation (ventricular diastole)

q: Which term matches this definition? “period of time when the heart muscle is relaxed and the chambers fill with blood”
why: diastole: period of time when the heart muscle is relaxed and the chambers fill with blood

q: Which term matches this definition? “(also, preload) the amount of blood in the ventricles at the end of atrial systole just prior to ventricular contraction”
