why: heart sounds: sounds heard via auscultation with a stethoscope of the closing of the atrioventricular valves (“lub”) and semilunar valves (“dub”)

q: Which term matches this definition? “(also, isovolumetric contraction) initial phase of ventricular contraction in which tension and pressure in the ventricle increase, but no blood is pumped or ejected from the heart”
why: isovolumic contraction: (also, isovolumetric contraction) initial phase of ventricular contraction in which tension and pressure in the ventricle increase, but no blood is pumped or ejected from the heart

q: The force the heart must overcome to pump blood is known as ________.
why: The correct answer is: afterload. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The cardiovascular centers are located in which area of the brain?
why: The correct answer is: medulla oblongata. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: In a healthy young adult, what happens to cardiac output when heart rate increases above 160 bpm?
options: There is no way to predict.
why: The correct answer is: It decreases.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What happens to preload when there is venous constriction in the veins?
options: There is no way to predict.
why: The correct answer is: It increases.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is a positive inotrope?
why: The correct answer is: Ca²⁺. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Why does increasing EDV increase contractility?
card.a: Increasing EDV increases the sarcomeres’ lengths within the cardiac muscle cells, allowing more cross bridge formation between the myosin and actin and providing for a more powerful contraction. This relationship is described in the Frank-Starling mechanism.

card.q: Why is afterload important to cardiac function?
card.a: Afterload represents the resistance within the arteries to the flow of blood ejected from the ventricles. If uncompensated, if afterload increases, flow will decrease. In order for the heart to maintain adequate flow to overcome increasing afterload, it must pump more forcefully. This is one of the negative consequences of high blood pressure or hypertension.

q: The earliest organ to form and begin function within the developing human is the ________.
why: The correct answer is: heart. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Of the three germ layers that give rise to all adult tissues and organs, which gives rise to the heart?
why: The correct answer is: mesoderm. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The two tubes that eventually fuse to form the heart are referred to as the ________.
why: The correct answer is: cardiogenic tubes. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which primitive area of the heart will give rise to the right ventricle?
why: The correct answer is: bulbus cordis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The pulmonary trunk and aorta are derived from which primitive heart structure?
why: The correct answer is: truncus arteriosus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Why is it so important for the human heart to develop early and begin functioning within the developing embryo?
card.a: The human embryo is rapidly growing and has great demands for nutrients and oxygen, while producing waste products including carbon dioxide. All of these materials must be received from or delivered to the mother for processing. Without an efficient early circulatory system, this would be impossible.

card.q: Describe how the major pumping chambers, the ventricles, form within the developing heart.
card.a: After fusion of the two endocardial tubes into the single primitive heart, five regions quickly become visible. From the head, these are the truncus arteriosus, bulbus cordis, primitive ventricle, primitive atrium, and sinus venosus. Contractions propel the blood from the sinus venosus to the truncus arteriosus. About day 23, the heart begins to form an S-shaped structure within the pericardium. The bulbus cordis develops into the right ventricle, whereas the primitive ventricle becomes the left ventricle. The interventricular septum separating these begins to form about day 28. The atrioventricular valves form between weeks five to eight. At this point, the heart ventricles resemble the adult structure.

q: The endothelium is found in the ________.
why: The correct answer is: tunica intima. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Nervi vasorum control ________.
why: The correct answer is: both vasoconstriction and vasodilation. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Closer to the heart, arteries would be expected to have a higher percentage of ________.
why: The correct answer is: elastic fibers. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following best describes veins?
options: thick walled, small lumens, low pressure, lack valves
thin walled, large lumens, low pressure, have valves
thin walled, small lumens, high pressure, have valves
thick walled, large lumens, high pressure, lack valves
why: The correct answer is: thin walled, large lumens, low pressure, have valves. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: An especially leaky type of capillary found in the liver and certain other tissues is called a ________.
why: The correct answer is: sinusoid capillary. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Arterioles are often referred to as resistance vessels. Why?
card.a: Arterioles receive blood from arteries, which are vessels with a much larger lumen. As their own lumen averages just 30 micrometers or less, arterioles are critical in slowing down—or resisting—blood flow. The arterioles can also constrict or dilate, which varies their resistance, to help distribute blood flow to the tissues.

card.q: Cocaine use causes vasoconstriction. Is this likely to increase or decrease blood pressure, and why?
card.a: Vasoconstriction causes the lumens of blood vessels to narrow. This increases the pressure of the blood flowing within the vessel.

card.q: A blood vessel with a few smooth muscle fibers and connective tissue, and only a very thin tunica externa conducts blood toward the heart. What type of vessel is this?
card.a: This is a venule.

q: In a blood pressure measurement of 110/70, the number 70 is the ________.
why: The correct answer is: diastolic pressure. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A healthy elastic artery ________.
options: has a thin wall and irregular lumen
why: The correct answer is: is compliant. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following statements is true?
options: The longer the vessel, the lower the resistance and the greater the flow.
As blood volume decreases, blood pressure and blood flow also decrease.
All of the above are true.
why: The correct answer is: As blood volume decreases, blood pressure and blood flow also decrease.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Slight vasodilation in an arteriole prompts a ________.
why: The correct answer is: huge decrease in resistance. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Venoconstriction increases which of the following?
options: return of blood to the heart
why: The correct answer is: all of the above. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: You measure a patient’s blood pressure at 130/85. Calculate the patient’s pulse pressure and mean arterial pressure. Determine whether each pressure is low, normal, or high.
card.a: The patient’s pulse pressure is 130 – 85 = 45 mm Hg. Generally, a pulse pressure should be at least 25 percent of the systolic pressure, but not more than 100 mm Hg. Since 25 percent of 130 = 32.5, the patient’s pulse pressure of 45 is normal. The patient’s mean arterial pressure is 85 + 1/3 (45) = 85 + 15 = 100. Normally, the mean arterial blood pressure falls within the range of 70 – 110 mmHg, so 100 is normal.

card.q: An obese patient comes to the clinic complaining of swollen feet and ankles, fatigue, shortness of breath, and often feeling “spaced out.” She is a cashier in a grocery store, a job that requires her to stand all day. Outside of work, she engages in no physical activity. She confesses that, because of her weight, she finds even walking uncomfortable. Explain how the skeletal muscle pump might play a role in this patient’s signs and symptoms.
card.a: People who stand upright all day and are inactive overall have very little skeletal muscle activity in the legs. Pooling of blood in the legs and feet is common. Venous return to the heart is reduced, a condition that in turn reduces cardiac output and therefore oxygenation of tissues throughout the body. This could at least partially account for the patient’s fatigue and shortness of breath, as well as her “spaced out” feeling, which commonly reflects reduced oxygen to the brain.

q: Hydrostatic pressure is ________.
options: greater than colloid osmotic pressure at the venous end of the capillary bed
the pressure exerted by fluid in an enclosed space
about zero at the midpoint of a capillary bed
why: The correct answer is: the pressure exerted by fluid in an enclosed space. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Net filtration pressure is calculated by ________.
options: adding the capillary hydrostatic pressure to the interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure
subtracting the fluid drained by the lymphatic vessels from the total fluid in the interstitial fluid
adding the blood colloid osmotic pressure to the capillary hydrostatic pressure
subtracting the blood colloid osmotic pressure from the capillary hydrostatic pressure
why: The correct answer is: subtracting the blood colloid osmotic pressure from the capillary hydrostatic pressure. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following statements is true?
options: In one day, more fluid exits the capillary through filtration than enters through reabsorption.
In one day, approximately 35 mm of blood are filtered and 7 mm are reabsorbed.
In one day, the capillaries of the lymphatic system absorb about 20.4 liters of fluid.
None of the above are true.
why: The correct answer is: In one day, more fluid exits the capillary through filtration than enters through reabsorption.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “pressure exerted by colloids suspended in blood within a vessel; a primary determinant is the presence of plasma proteins”
why: blood colloidal osmotic pressure (BCOP): pressure exerted by colloids suspended in blood within a vessel; a primary determinant is the presence of plasma proteins

q: Which term matches this definition? “force blood exerts against the walls of a blood vessel or heart chamber”
why: blood hydrostatic pressure: force blood exerts against the walls of a blood vessel or heart chamber

q: Which term matches this definition? “force blood exerts against a capillary”
why: capillary hydrostatic pressure (CHP): force blood exerts against a capillary

q: Which term matches this definition? “in the cardiovascular system, the movement of material from a capillary into the interstitial fluid, moving from an area of higher pressure to lower pressure”
why: filtration: in the cardiovascular system, the movement of material from a capillary into the interstitial fluid, moving from an area of higher pressure to lower pressure

q: Which term matches this definition? “pressure exerted by the colloids within the interstitial fluid”
why: interstitial fluid colloidal osmotic pressure (IFCOP): pressure exerted by the colloids within the interstitial fluid

q: Which term matches this definition? “force exerted by the fluid in the tissue spaces”
why: interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure (IFHP): force exerted by the fluid in the tissue spaces

card.q: A patient arrives at the emergency department with dangerously low blood pressure. The patient’s blood colloid osmotic pressure is normal. How would you expect this situation to affect the patient’s net filtration pressure?
card.a: The patient’s blood would flow more sluggishly from the arteriole into the capillary bed. Thus, the patient’s capillary hydrostatic pressure would be below the normal 35 mm Hg at the arterial end. At the same time, the patient’s blood colloidal osmotic pressure is normal—about 25 mm Hg. Thus, even at the arterial end of the capillary bed, the net filtration pressure would be below 10 mm Hg, and an abnormally reduced level of filtration would occur. In fact, reabsorption might begin to occur by the midpoint of the capillary bed.

card.q: True or false? The plasma proteins suspended in blood cross the capillary cell membrane and enter the tissue fluid via facilitated diffusion. Explain your thinking.
card.a: False. The plasma proteins suspended in blood cannot cross the semipermeable capillary cell membrane, and so they remain in the plasma within the vessel, where they account for the blood colloid osmotic pressure.

q: Clusters of neurons in the medulla oblongata that regulate blood pressure are known collectively as ________.
why: The correct answer is: the cardiovascular center. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: In the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone mechanism, ________.
options: decreased blood pressure prompts the release of renin from the liver
aldosterone prompts the kidneys to reabsorb sodium
why: The correct answer is: aldosterone prompts the kidneys to reabsorb sodium. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: In the myogenic response, ________.
options: muscle contraction promotes venous return to the heart
vascular smooth muscle responds to stretch
why: The correct answer is: vascular smooth muscle responds to stretch. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A form of circulatory shock common in young children with severe diarrhea or vomiting is ________.
why: The correct answer is: hypovolemic shock. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “type of shock that follows a severe allergic reaction and results from massive vasodilation”
why: anaphylactic shock: type of shock that follows a severe allergic reaction and results from massive vasodilation

q: Which term matches this definition? “small pockets in the ascending aorta near the aortic valve that are the locations of the baroreceptors (stretch receptors) and chemoreceptors that trigger a reflex that aids in the regulation of vascular homeostasis”
why: aortic sinuses: small pockets in the ascending aorta near the aortic valve that are the locations of the baroreceptors (stretch receptors) and chemoreceptors that trigger a reflex that aids in the regulation of vascular homeostasis

q: Which term matches this definition? “type of shock that results from the inability of the heart to maintain cardiac output”
why: cardiogenic shock: type of shock that results from the inability of the heart to maintain cardiac output

q: Which term matches this definition? “small pockets near the base of the internal carotid arteries that are the locations of the baroreceptors and chemoreceptors that trigger a reflex that aids in the regulation of vascular homeostasis”
why: carotid sinuses: small pockets near the base of the internal carotid arteries that are the locations of the baroreceptors and chemoreceptors that trigger a reflex that aids in the regulation of vascular homeostasis

q: Which term matches this definition? “also simply called shock; a life-threatening medical condition in which the circulatory system is unable to supply enough blood flow to provide adequate oxygen and other nutrients to the tissues to maintain cellular metabolism”
why: circulatory shock: also simply called shock; a life-threatening medical condition in which the circulatory system is unable to supply enough blood flow to provide adequate oxygen and other nutrients to the tissues to maintain cellular metabolism

q: Which term matches this definition? “chronic and persistent blood pressure measurements of 140/90 mm Hg or above”
why: hypertension: chronic and persistent blood pressure measurements of 140/90 mm Hg or above

card.q: Listen to this podcast to learn about hypertension, often described as a “silent killer.” What steps can you take to reduce your risk of a heart attack or stroke?
card.a: Take medications as prescribed, eat a healthy diet, exercise, and don’t smoke.

card.q: A patient arrives in the emergency department with a blood pressure of 70/45 confused and complaining of thirst. Why?
card.a: This blood pressure is insufficient to circulate blood throughout the patient’s body and maintain adequate perfusion of the patient’s tissues. Ischemia would prompt hypoxia, including to the brain, prompting confusion. The low blood pressure would also trigger the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone mechanism, and release of aldosterone would stimulate the thirst mechanism in the hypothalamus.

card.q: Nitric oxide is broken down very quickly after its release. Why?
card.a: Nitric oxide is a very powerful local vasodilator that is important in the autoregulation of tissue perfusion. If it were not broken down very quickly after its release, blood flow to the region could exceed metabolic needs.

q: The coronary arteries branch off of the ________.
why: The correct answer is: ascending aorta. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following statements is true?
options: The left and right common carotid arteries both branch off of the brachiocephalic trunk.
The brachial artery is the distal branch of the axillary artery.
The radial and ulnar arteries join to form the palmar arch.
All of the above are true.
why: The correct answer is: The radial and ulnar arteries join to form the palmar arch.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Arteries serving the stomach, pancreas, and liver all branch from the ________.
why: The correct answer is: celiac trunk. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The right and left brachiocephalic veins ________.
options: drain blood from the right and left internal jugular veins
drain blood from the right and left subclavian veins
drain into the superior vena cava
all of the above are true
why: The correct answer is: all of the above are true. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The hepatic portal system delivers blood from the digestive organs to the ________.
why: The correct answer is: liver. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Identify the ventricle of the heart that pumps oxygen-depleted blood and the arteries of the body that carry oxygen-depleted blood.
card.a: The right ventricle of the heart pumps oxygen-depleted blood to the pulmonary arteries.

card.q: What organs do the gonadal veins drain?
card.a: The gonadal veins drain the testes in males and the ovaries in females.

card.q: What arteries play the leading roles in supplying blood to the brain?
card.a: The internal carotid arteries and the vertebral arteries provide most of the brain’s blood supply.

q: Blood islands are ________.
options: clusters of blood-filtering cells in the placenta
masses of pluripotent stem cells scattered throughout the fetal bone marrow
vascular tubes that give rise to the embryonic tubular heart
masses of developing blood vessels and formed elements scattered throughout the embryonic disc
why: The correct answer is: masses of developing blood vessels and formed elements scattered throughout the embryonic disc. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following statements is true?
options: Two umbilical veins carry oxygen-depleted blood from the fetal circulation to the placenta.
One umbilical vein carries oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetal heart.
Two umbilical arteries carry oxygen-depleted blood to the fetal lungs.
None of the above are true.
why: The correct answer is: One umbilical vein carries oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetal heart.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The ductus venosus is a shunt that allows ________.
options: fetal blood to flow from the right atrium to the left atrium
fetal blood to flow from the right ventricle to the left ventricle
most freshly oxygenated blood to flow into the fetal heart
most oxygen-depleted fetal blood to flow directly into the fetal pulmonary trunk
why: The correct answer is: most freshly oxygenated blood to flow into the fetal heart. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “stem cells that give rise to blood vessels”
why: angioblasts: stem cells that give rise to blood vessels

q: Which term matches this definition? “development of new blood vessels from existing vessels”
why: angiogenesis: development of new blood vessels from existing vessels

q: Which term matches this definition? “masses of developing blood vessels and formed elements from mesodermal cells scattered throughout the embryonic disc”
why: blood islands: masses of developing blood vessels and formed elements from mesodermal cells scattered throughout the embryonic disc

q: Which term matches this definition? “shunt in the fetal pulmonary trunk that diverts oxygenated blood back to the aorta”
why: ductus arteriosus: shunt in the fetal pulmonary trunk that diverts oxygenated blood back to the aorta

q: Which term matches this definition? “shunt that causes oxygenated blood to bypass the fetal liver on its way to the inferior vena cava”
why: ductus venosus: shunt that causes oxygenated blood to bypass the fetal liver on its way to the inferior vena cava

q: Which term matches this definition? “shunt that directly connects the right and left atria and helps to divert oxygenated blood from the fetal pulmonary circuit”
why: foramen ovale: shunt that directly connects the right and left atria and helps to divert oxygenated blood from the fetal pulmonary circuit

card.q: All tissues, including malignant tumors, need a blood supply. Explain why drugs called angiogenesis inhibitors would be used in cancer treatment.
card.a: Angiogenesis inhibitors are drugs that inhibit the growth of new blood vessels. They can impede the growth of tumors by limiting their blood supply and therefore their access to gas and nutrient exchange.

card.q: Explain the location and importance of the ductus arteriosus in fetal circulation.
card.a: The ductus arteriosus is a blood vessel that provides a passageway between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta during fetal life. Most blood ejected from the fetus’ right ventricle and entering the pulmonary trunk is diverted through this structure into the fetal aorta, thus bypassing the fetal lungs.

q: Which of the following cells is phagocytic?
why: The correct answer is: macrophage. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which structure allows lymph from the lower right limb to enter the bloodstream?
why: The correct answer is: thoracic duct. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following cells is important in the innate immune response?
why: The correct answer is: macrophages. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following cells would be most active in early, antiviral immune responses the first time one is exposed to pathogen?
why: The correct answer is: natural killer cell. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the lymphoid nodules is most likely to see food antigens first?
why: The correct answer is: tonsils. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Visit this website for an overview of the lymphatic system. What are the three main components of the lymphatic system?
card.a: The three main components are the lymph vessels, the lymph nodes, and the lymph.

card.q: Visit this website to learn about the many different cell types in the immune system and their very specialized jobs. What is the role of the dendritic cell in infection by HIV?
card.a: The dendritic cell transports the virus to a lymph node.

card.q: Describe the flow of lymph from its origins in interstitial fluid to its emptying into the venous bloodstream.
card.a: The lymph enters through lymphatic capillaries, and then into larger lymphatic vessels. The lymph can only go in one direction due to valves in the vessels. The larger lymphatics merge to form trunks that enter into the blood via lymphatic ducts.

q: Which of the following signs is not characteristic of inflammation?
why: The correct answer is: cold. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is not important in the antiviral innate immune response?
why: The correct answer is: microphages. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Enhanced phagocytosis of a cell by the binding of a specific protein is called ________.
why: The correct answer is: opsonization. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following leads to the redness of inflammation?
why: The correct answer is: increased blood flow. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “inflammation occurring for a limited time period; rapidly developing”
why: acute inflammation: inflammation occurring for a limited time period; rapidly developing

q: Which term matches this definition? “soluble, long-range, cell-to-cell communication molecule”
why: chemokine: soluble, long-range, cell-to-cell communication molecule

q: Which term matches this definition? “inflammation occurring for long periods of time”
why: chronic inflammation: inflammation occurring for long periods of time

q: Which term matches this definition? “enzymatic cascade of constitutive blood proteins that have antipathogen effects, including the direct killing of bacteria”
why: complement: enzymatic cascade of constitutive blood proteins that have antipathogen effects, including the direct killing of bacteria

q: Which term matches this definition? “soluble, short-range, cell-to-cell communication molecule”
why: cytokine: soluble, short-range, cell-to-cell communication molecule

q: Which term matches this definition? “includes antimicrobial proteins stimulated during the first several days of an infection”
why: early induced immune response: includes antimicrobial proteins stimulated during the first several days of an infection

card.q: Visit this website to learn about phagocyte chemotaxis. Phagocyte chemotaxis is the movement of phagocytes according to the secretion of chemical messengers in the form of interleukins and other chemokines. By what means does a phagocyte destroy a bacterium that it has ingested?
card.a: The bacterium is digested by the phagocyte’s digestive enzymes (contained in its lysosomes).

card.q: Describe the process of inflammation in an area that has been traumatized, but not infected.
card.a: The cell debris and damaged cells induce macrophages to begin to clean them up. Macrophages release cytokines that attract neutrophils, followed by more macrophages. Other mediators released by mast cells increase blood flow to the area and also vascular permeability, allowing the recruited cells to get from the blood to the site of infection, where they can phagocytose the dead cells and debris, preparing the site for wound repair.

card.q: Describe two early induced responses and what pathogens they affect.
card.a: Interferons are produced in virally infected cells and cause them to secrete signals for surrounding cells to make antiviral proteins. C-reactive protein is induced to be made by the liver and will opsonize certain species of bacteria.

q: T cells that secrete cytokines that help antibody responses are called ________.
why: The correct answer is: Th2. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The taking in of antigen and digesting it for later presentation is called ________.
why: The correct answer is: antigen processing. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Why is clonal expansion so important?
options: to increase the numbers of specific cells
why: The correct answer is: to increase the numbers of specific cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The elimination of self-reactive thymocytes is called ________.
why: The correct answer is: negative selection.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which type of T cell is most effective against viruses?
why: The correct answer is: cytotoxic T cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Describe the processing and presentation of an intracellular antigen.
card.a: The antigen is digested by the proteasome, brought into the endoplasmic reticulum by the TAP transporter system, where it binds to class I MHC molecules. These are taken to the cell surface by transport vesicles.

card.q: Describe clonal selection and expansion.
card.a: Antigen-specific clones are stimulated as their antigen receptor binds to antigen. They are then activated and proliferate, expanding their numbers. The result is a large number of antigen-specific lymphocytes.

q: Removing functionality from a B cell without killing it is called ________.
why: The correct answer is: clonal anergy. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which class of antibody crosses the placenta in pregnant people?
why: The correct answer is: IgG. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which class of antibody has no known function other than as an antigen receptor?
why: The correct answer is: IgD. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: When does class switching occur?
why: The correct answer is: primary response. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which class of antibody is found in mucus?
why: The correct answer is: IgA. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Immunity can be acquired in an active or passive way, and it can be natural or artificial. Watch this video to see an animated discussion of passive and active immunity. What is an example of natural immunity acquired passively?
card.a: Breastfeeding is an example of natural immunity acquired passively.

card.q: Describe how secondary B cell responses are developed.
card.a: B cells activated during a primary response differentiate either into terminally differentiated plasma cells or into memory B cells. These memory B cells are what respond during a secondary or memory antibody response.

card.q: Describe the role of IgM in immunity.
card.a: IgM is an antigen receptor on naïve B cells. Upon activation, naïve B cells make IgM first. IgM is good at binding complement and thus has good antibacterial effects. IgM is replaced with other classes of antibodies later on in the primary response due to class switching.

q: Which enzymes in macrophages are important for clearing intracellular bacteria?
why: The correct answer is: lysosomal. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What type of chronic lung disease is caused by a Mycobacterium?
why: The correct answer is: tuberculosis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which type of immune response is most directly effective against bacteria?
why: The correct answer is: complement. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the reason that you have to be immunized with a new influenza vaccine each year?
options: the vaccine is only protective for a year
why: The correct answer is: mutation. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which type of immune response works in concert with cytotoxic T cells against virally infected cells?
why: The correct answer is: natural killer cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Describe how seroconversion works in HIV disease.
card.a: Seroconversion is the clearance of virus in the serum due to the increase in specific serum antibody levels. Seroconversion happens in the early stages of HIV disease. Unfortunately, the antibody cannot completely clear the virus from the body and thus it most often progresses to AIDS.

card.q: Describe tuberculosis and the innocent bystander effect.
card.a: Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria resistant to lysosomal enzymes in alveolar macrophages, resulting in chronic infection. The immune response to these bacteria actually causes most of the lung damage that is characteristic of this life-threatening disease.

q: Which type of hypersensitivity involves soluble antigen-antibody complexes?
why: The correct answer is: type III. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What causes the delay in delayed hypersensitivity?
why: The correct answer is: recruitment of immune cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is a critical feature of immediate hypersensitivity?
why: The correct answer is: histamine release. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is an autoimmune disease of the heart?
why: The correct answer is: rheumatic fever. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What drug is used to counteract the effects of anaphylactic shock?
why: The correct answer is: epinephrine. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Describe anaphylactic shock in someone sensitive to peanuts?
card.a: The peanuts cause high levels of mast cell degranulation in the throats of these individuals. The histamine released increases vascular permeability, causing edema and (swelling), making breathing difficult. This must be treated with epinephrine as soon as possible.

card.q: Describe rheumatic fever and how tolerance is broken.
card.a: Antibody response to the cell walls of β-Streptococcus cross-reacts with the heart muscle. Complement is then activated and the heart is damaged, leading to abnormal function. Tolerance is broken because heart myosin antigens are similar to antigens on the β- Streptococcus bacteria.

q: Which of the following terms means “many genes”?
why: The correct answer is: polygeny. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Why do we have natural antibodies?
why: The correct answer is: immunity to environmental bacteria. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which type of cancer is associated with HIV disease?
why: The correct answer is: Kaposi’s sarcoma. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: How does cyclosporine A work?
why: The correct answer is: suppresses T cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What disease is associated with bone marrow transplants?
why: The correct answer is: graft-versus-host disease. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Describe how stress affects immune responses.
card.a: Stress causes the release of hormones and the activation of nerves that suppress the immune response. Short-term stress has little effect on the health of an already healthy individual, whereas chronic stress does lead to increases in disease in such people.

q: Which of the following anatomical structures is not part of the conducting zone?
why: The correct answer is: alveoli. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the function of the conchae in the nasal cavity?
why: The correct answer is: increase surface area. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The fauces connects which of the following structures to the oropharynx?
why: The correct answer is: oral cavity. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following are structural features of the trachea?
why: The correct answer is: all of the above. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following structures is the most distal (or last) component of the bronchial tree?
why: The correct answer is: alveoli. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the role of alveolar macrophages?
why: The correct answer is: to remove pathogens and debris. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Visit this site to learn more about what happens during an asthma attack. What are the three changes that occur inside the airways during an asthma attack?
card.a: Inflammation and the production of a thick mucus; constriction of the airway muscles, or bronchospasm; and an increased sensitivity to allergens.

card.q: Describe the three regions of the pharynx and their functions.
card.a: The pharynx has three major regions. The first region is the nasopharynx, which is connected to the posterior nasal cavity and functions as an airway. The second region is the oropharynx, which is continuous with the nasopharynx and is connected to the oral cavity at the fauces. The laryngopharynx is connected to the oropharynx and the esophagus and trachea. Both the oropharynx and laryngopharynx are passageways for air and food and drink.

card.q: If a person sustains an injury to the epiglottis, what would be the physiological result?
card.a: The epiglottis is a region of the larynx that is important during the swallowing of food or drink. As a person swallows, the pharynx moves upward and the epiglottis closes over the trachea, preventing food or drink from entering the trachea. If a person’s epiglottis were injured, this mechanism would be impaired. As a result, the person may have problems with food or drink entering the trachea, and possibly, the lungs. Over time, this may cause infections such as pneumonia to set in.

card.q: Compare and contrast the conducting and respiratory zones.
card.a: The conducting zone of the respiratory system includes the organs and structures that are not directly involved in gas exchange, but perform other duties such as providing a passageway for air, trapping and removing debris and pathogens, and warming and humidifying incoming air. Such structures include the nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, and most of the bronchial tree. The respiratory zone includes all the organs and structures that are directly involved in gas exchange, including the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli.

q: Which of the following structures separates the lung into lobes?
why: The correct answer is: fissure. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A section of the lung that receives its own tertiary bronchus is called the ________.
why: The correct answer is: bronchopulmonary segment. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The ________ circulation picks up oxygen for cellular use and drops off carbon dioxide for removal from the body.
why: The correct answer is: respiratory. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The pleura that surrounds the lungs consists of two layers, the ________.
why: The correct answer is: visceral and parietal pleurae.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “decrease in the size of the bronchiole due to contraction of the muscular wall”
why: bronchoconstriction: decrease in the size of the bronchiole due to contraction of the muscular wall

q: Which term matches this definition? “increase in the size of the bronchiole due to relaxation of the muscular wall”
why: bronchodilation: increase in the size of the bronchiole due to relaxation of the muscular wall

q: Which term matches this definition? “indentation on the surface of the left lung that allows space for the heart”
why: cardiac notch: indentation on the surface of the left lung that allows space for the heart

q: Which term matches this definition? “concave structure on the mediastinal surface of the lungs where blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, nerves, and a bronchus enter the lung”
why: hilum: concave structure on the mediastinal surface of the lungs where blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, nerves, and a bronchus enter the lung

q: Which term matches this definition? “organ of the respiratory system that performs gas exchange”
why: lung: organ of the respiratory system that performs gas exchange

q: Which term matches this definition? “outermost layer of the pleura that connects to the thoracic wall, mediastinum, and diaphragm”
why: parietal pleura: outermost layer of the pleura that connects to the thoracic wall, mediastinum, and diaphragm

card.q: Compare and contrast the right and left lungs.
card.a: The right and left lungs differ in size and shape to accommodate other organs that encroach on the thoracic region. The right lung consists of three lobes and is shorter than the left lung, due to the position of the liver underneath it. The left lung consist of two lobes and is longer and narrower than the right lung. The left lung has a concave region on the mediastinal surface called the cardiac notch that allows space for the heart.

card.q: Why are the pleurae not damaged during normal breathing?
card.a: There is a cavity, called the pleural cavity, between the parietal and visceral layers of the pleura. Mesothelial cells produce and secrete pleural fluid into the pleural cavity that acts as a lubricant. Therefore, as you breathe, the pleural fluid prevents the two layers of the pleura from rubbing against each other and causing damage due to friction.

q: Which of the following processes does atmospheric pressure play a role in?
why: The correct answer is: pulmonary ventilation. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A decrease in volume leads to a(n) ________ pressure.
why: The correct answer is: increase in. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The pressure difference between the intra-alveolar and intrapleural pressures is called ________.
why: The correct answer is: transpulmonary pressure. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Watch this video to learn more about lung volumes and spirometers. Explain how spirometry test results can be used to diagnose respiratory diseases or determine the effectiveness of disease treatment.
card.a: Patients with respiratory ailments (such as asthma, emphysema, COPD, etc.) have issues with airway resistance and/or lung compliance. Both of these factors can interfere with the patient’s ability to move air effectively. A spirometry test can determine how much air the patient can move into and out of the lungs. If the air volumes are low, this can indicate that the patient has a respiratory disease or that the treatment regimen may need to be adjusted. If the numbers are normal, the patient does not have a significant respiratory disease or the treatment regimen is working as expected.

card.q: Describe what is meant by the term “lung compliance.”
card.a: Lung compliance refers to the ability of lung tissue to stretch under pressure, which is determined in part by the surface tension of the alveoli and the ability of the connective tissue to stretch. Lung compliance plays a role in determining how much the lungs can change in volume, which in turn helps to determine pressure and air movement.

card.q: What is respiratory rate and how is it controlled?
card.a: Respiratory rate is defined as the number of breaths taken per minute. Respiratory rate is controlled by the respiratory center, located in the medulla oblongata. Conscious thought can alter the normal respiratory rate through control by skeletal muscle, although one cannot consciously stop the rate altogether. A typical resting respiratory rate is about 14 breaths per minute.

card.q: Compare and contrast Dalton’s law and Henry’s law.
card.a: Both Dalton’s and Henry’s laws describe the behavior of gases. Dalton’s law states that any gas in a mixture of gases exerts force as if it were not in a mixture. Henry’s law states that gas molecules dissolve in a liquid proportional to their partial pressure.

card.q: A smoker develops damage to several alveoli that then can no longer function. How does this affect gas exchange?
card.a: The damaged alveoli will have insufficient ventilation, causing the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli to decrease. As a result, the pulmonary capillaries serving these alveoli will constrict, redirecting blood flow to other alveoli that are receiving sufficient ventilation.

card.q: Watch this video to see the transport of oxygen from the lungs to the tissues. Why is oxygenated blood bright red, whereas deoxygenated blood tends to be more of a purple color?
card.a: When oxygen binds to the hemoglobin molecule, oxyhemoglobin is created, which has a red color to it. Hemoglobin that is not bound to oxygen tends to be more of a blue–purple color. Oxygenated blood traveling through the systemic arteries has large amounts of oxyhemoglobin. As blood passes through the tissues, much of the oxygen is released into systemic capillaries. The deoxygenated blood returning through the systemic veins, therefore, contains much smaller amounts of oxyhemoglobin. The more oxyhemoglobin that is present in the blood, the redder the fluid will be. As a result, oxygenated blood will be much redder in color than deoxygenated blood.

card.q: Compare and contrast adult hemoglobin and fetal hemoglobin.
card.a: Both adult and fetal hemoglobin transport oxygen via iron molecules. However, fetal hemoglobin has about a 20-fold greater affinity for oxygen than does adult hemoglobin. This is due to a difference in structure; fetal hemoglobin has two subunits that have a slightly different structure than the subunits of adult hemoglobin.

card.q: Describe the relationship between the partial pressure of oxygen and the binding of oxygen to hemoglobin.
card.a: The relationship between the partial pressure of oxygen and the binding of hemoglobin to oxygen is described by the oxygen–hemoglobin saturation/dissociation curve. As the partial pressure of oxygen increases, the number of oxygen molecules bound by hemoglobin increases, thereby increasing the saturation of hemoglobin.

card.q: Describe three ways in which carbon dioxide can be transported.
card.a: Carbon dioxide can be transported by three mechanisms: dissolved in plasma, as bicarbonate, or as carbaminohemoglobin. Dissolved in plasma, carbon dioxide molecules simply diffuse into the blood from the tissues. Bicarbonate is created by a chemical reaction that occurs mostly in erythrocytes, joining carbon dioxide and water by carbonic anhydrase, producing carbonic acid, which breaks down into bicarbonate and hydrogen ions. Carbaminohemoglobin is the bound form of hemoglobin and carbon dioxide.

card.q: Describe the neural factors involved in increasing ventilation during exercise.
card.a: There are three neural factors that play a role in the increased ventilation observed during exercise. Because this increased ventilation occurs at the beginning of exercise, it is unlikely that only blood oxygen and carbon dioxide levels are involved. The first neural factor is the psychological stimulus of making a conscious decision to exercise. The second neural factor is the stimulus of motor neuron activation by the skeletal muscles, which are involved in exercise. The third neural factor is activation of the proprioceptors located in the muscles, joints, and tendons that stimulate activity in the respiratory centers.

card.q: What is the major mechanism that results in acclimatization?
card.a: A major mechanism involved in acclimatization is the increased production of erythrocytes. A drop in tissue levels of oxygen stimulates the kidneys to produce the hormone erythropoietin, which signals the bone marrow to produce erythrocytes. As a result, individuals exposed to a high altitude for long periods of time have a greater number of circulating erythrocytes than do individuals at lower altitudes.

card.q: During what timeframe does a fetus have enough mature structures to breathe on its own if born prematurely? Describe the other structures that develop during this phase.
card.a: At about week 28, enough alveolar precursors have matured so that a baby born prematurely at this time can usually breathe on its own. Other structures that develop about this time are pulmonary capillaries, expanding to create a large surface area for gas exchange. Alveolar ducts and alveolar precursors have also developed.

card.q: Describe fetal breathing movements and their purpose.
card.a: Fetal breathing movements occur due to the contraction of respiratory muscles, causing the fetus to inhale and exhale amniotic fluid. It is thought that these movements are a way to “practice” breathing, which results in toning the muscles in preparation for breathing after birth. In addition, fetal breathing movements may help alveoli to form and mature.

card.q: Explain how the enteric nervous system supports the digestive system. What might occur that could result in the autonomic nervous system having a negative impact on digestion?
card.a: The enteric nervous system helps regulate alimentary canal motility and the secretion of digestive juices, thus facilitating digestion. If a person becomes overly anxious, sympathetic innervation of the alimentary canal is stimulated, which can result in a slowing of digestive activity.

card.q: The composition of saliva varies from gland to gland. Discuss how saliva produced by the parotid gland differs in action from saliva produced by the sublingual gland.
card.a: Parotid gland saliva is watery with little mucus but a lot of amylase, which allows it to mix freely with food during mastication and begin the digestion of carbohydrates. In contrast, sublingual gland saliva has a lot of mucus with the least amount of amylase of all the salivary glands. The high mucus content serves to lubricate the food for swallowing.

card.q: During a hockey game, the puck hits a player in the mouth, knocking out all eight of their most anterior teeth. Which teeth did the player lose and how does this loss affect food ingestion?
card.a: The incisors. Since these teeth are used for tearing off pieces of food during ingestion, the player will need to ingest foods that have already been cut into bite-sized pieces until the broken teeth are replaced.

card.q: What prevents swallowed food from entering the airways?
card.a: Usually when food is swallowed, involuntary muscle contractions cause the soft palate to rise and close off the nasopharynx. The larynx also is pulled up, and the epiglottis folds over the glottis. These actions block off the air passages.

card.q: Explain the mechanism responsible for gastroesophageal reflux.
card.a: If the lower esophageal sphincter does not close completely, the stomach’s acidic contents can back up into the esophagus, a phenomenon known as GERD.

card.q: Describe the three processes involved in the esophageal phase of deglutition.
card.a: Peristalsis moves the bolus down the esophagus and toward the stomach. Esophageal glands secrete mucus that lubricates the bolus and reduces friction. When the bolus nears the stomach, the lower esophageal sphincter relaxes, allowing the bolus to pass into the stomach.

card.q: Explain how the stomach is protected from self-digestion and why this is necessary.
card.a: The mucosal barrier protects the stomach from self-digestion. It includes a thick coating of bicarbonate-rich mucus; the mucus is physically protective, and bicarbonate neutralizes gastric acid. Epithelial cells meet at tight junctions, which block gastric juice from penetrating the underlying tissue layers, and stem cells quickly replace sloughed off epithelial mucosal cells.

card.q: Describe unique anatomical features that enable the stomach to perform digestive functions.
card.a: The stomach has an additional inner oblique smooth muscle layer that helps the muscularis churn and mix food. The epithelium includes gastric glands that secrete gastric fluid. The gastric fluid consists mainly of mucous, HCl, and the enzyme pepsin released as pepsinogen.

card.q: Explain how nutrients absorbed in the small intestine pass into the general circulation.
card.a: Nutrients from the breakdown of carbohydrates and proteins are absorbed through a capillary bed in the villi of the small intestine. Lipid breakdown products are absorbed into a lacteal in the villi, and transported via the lymphatic system to the bloodstream.

card.q: Why is it important that chyme from the stomach is delivered to the small intestine slowly and in small amounts?

card.q: Describe three of the differences between the walls of the large and small intestines.

There are three features that are unique to the large intestine: teniae coli, haustra, and epiploic appendages.

card.q: Describe the location of hepatocytes in the liver and how this arrangement enhances their function.
