q: Which term matches this definition? “brush border enzyme that acts on proteins”
why: dipeptidase: brush border enzyme that acts on proteins

card.q: Explain the role of bile salts and lecithin in the emulsification of lipids (fats).
card.a: Bile salts and lecithin can emulsify large lipid globules because they are amphipathic; they have a nonpolar (hydrophobic) region that attaches to the large fat molecules as well as a polar (hydrophilic) region that interacts with the watery chime in the intestine.

card.q: How is vitamin B₁₂ absorbed?
card.a: Intrinsic factor secreted in the stomach binds to the large B₁₂ compound, creating a combination that can bind to mucosal receptors in the ileum.

q: A monosaccharide is formed from a polysaccharide in what kind of reaction?
why: The correct answer is: catabolic reaction. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: If anabolic reactions exceed catabolic reactions, the result will be ________.
why: The correct answer is: weight gain. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: When NAD becomes NADH, the coenzyme has been ________.
why: The correct answer is: reduced. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Anabolic reactions use energy by ________.
options: removing a phosphate group from ATP
breaking down molecules into smaller parts
why: The correct answer is: removing a phosphate group from ATP. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “hormones that stimulate the synthesis of new, larger molecules”
why: anabolic hormones: hormones that stimulate the synthesis of new, larger molecules

q: Which term matches this definition? “reactions that build smaller molecules into larger molecules”
why: anabolic reactions: reactions that build smaller molecules into larger molecules

q: Which term matches this definition? “reactions that create new molecules, also called anabolic reactions”
why: biosynthesis reactions: reactions that create new molecules, also called anabolic reactions

q: Which term matches this definition? “hormones that stimulate the breakdown of larger molecules”
why: catabolic hormones: hormones that stimulate the breakdown of larger molecules

q: Which term matches this definition? “reactions that break down larger molecules into their constituent parts”
why: catabolic reactions: reactions that break down larger molecules into their constituent parts

q: Which term matches this definition? “high-energy molecule needed for glycolysis”
why: FADH₂: high-energy molecule needed for glycolysis

card.q: Describe how metabolism can be altered.
card.a: An increase or decrease in lean muscle mass will result in an increase or decrease in metabolism.

card.q: Describe how Addison’s disease can be treated.
card.a: Addison’s disease is characterized by low cortisol levels. One way to treat the disease is by giving cortisol to the patient.

q: Glycolysis results in the production of two ________ molecules from a single molecule of glucose. In the absence of ________, the end product of glycolysis is ________.
why: The correct answer is: pyruvate, oxygen, lactate. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The Krebs cycle converts ________ through a cycle of reactions. In the process, ATP, ________, and ________ are produced.
why: The correct answer is: acetyl CoA; FADH₂; NADH. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which pathway produces the most ATP molecules?
why: The correct answer is: the electron transport chain. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Aerobic cellular respiration results in the production of these two products.
why: The correct answer is: ATP and H₂O. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: When NAD⁺ becomes NADH, the coenzyme has been ________.
why: The correct answer is: reduced. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Explain how glucose is metabolized to yield ATP.
card.a: Glucose is oxidized during glycolysis, creating pyruvate, which is processed through the Krebs cycle to produce NADH, FADH₂, ATP, and CO₂. The FADH₂ and NADH yield ATP.

card.q: Insulin is released when food is ingested and stimulates the uptake of glucose into the cell. Discuss the mechanism cells employ to create a concentration gradient to ensure continual uptake of glucose from the bloodstream.
card.a: Upon entry into the cell, hexokinase or glucokinase phosphorylates glucose, converting it into glucose-6-phosphate. In this form, glucose-6-phosphate is trapped in the cell. Because all of the glucose has been phosphorylated, new glucose molecules can be transported into the cell according to its concentration gradient.

q: Lipids in the diet can be ________.
options: broken down into energy for the body
stored as triglycerides for later use
why: The correct answer is: all of the above. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The gallbladder provides ________ that aid(s) in transport of lipids across the intestinal membrane.
why: The correct answer is: bile salts. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Triglycerides are transported by chylomicrons because ________.
options: they cannot move easily in the blood stream because they are fat based, while the blood is water based
they are too small to move by themselves
the chylomicrons contain enzymes they need for anabolism
they cannot fit across the intestinal membrane
why: The correct answer is: they cannot move easily in the blood stream because they are fat based, while the blood is water based. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which molecule produces the most ATP?
why: The correct answer is: triglycerides. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which molecules can enter the Krebs cycle?
why: The correct answer is: acetyl CoA. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Acetyl CoA can be converted to all of the following except ________.
why: The correct answer is: polysaccharides. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Discuss how carbohydrates can be stored as fat.
card.a: Carbohydrates are converted into pyruvate during glycolysis. This pyruvate is converted into acetyl CoA and proceeds through the Krebs cycle. When excess acetyl CoA is produced that cannot be processed through the Krebs cycle, the acetyl CoA is converted into triglycerides and fatty acids to be stored in the liver and adipose tissue.

card.q: If a person with diabetes that has breath smells like alcohol, what could this mean?
card.a: If diabetes is uncontrolled, the glucose in the blood is not being taken up and processed by the cells. Although blood glucose levels are high, there is no glucose available to the cells to be converted into energy. Because glucose is lacking, the body turns to other energy sources, including ketones. A side effect of using ketones as fuel is a sweet alcohol smell on the breath.

q: Digestion of proteins begins in the ________ where ________ and ________ mix with food to break down protein into ________.
why: The correct answer is: stomach; pepsin; HCl; amino acids. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Amino acids are needed to ________.
why: The correct answer is: build new proteins. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: If an amino acid is not used to create new proteins, it can be ________.
why: The correct answer is: converted to glucose or ketones. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “pancreatic enzyme that digests protein”
why: chymotrypsin: pancreatic enzyme that digests protein

q: Which term matches this definition? “proenzyme that is activated by trypsin into chymotrypsin”
why: chymotrypsinogen: proenzyme that is activated by trypsin into chymotrypsin

q: Which term matches this definition? “pancreatic enzyme that digests protein”
why: elastase: pancreatic enzyme that digests protein

q: Which term matches this definition? “enzyme located in the wall of the small intestine that activates trypsin”
why: enterokinase: enzyme located in the wall of the small intestine that activates trypsin

q: Which term matches this definition? “forms in which proteases are stored and released to prevent the inappropriate digestion of the native proteins of the stomach, pancreas, and small intestine”
why: inactive proenzymes: forms in which proteases are stored and released to prevent the inappropriate digestion of the native proteins of the stomach, pancreas, and small intestine

q: Which term matches this definition? “enzyme that begins to break down proteins in the stomach”
why: pepsin: enzyme that begins to break down proteins in the stomach

card.q: Amino acids are not stored in the body. Describe how excess amino acids are processed in the cell.
card.a: Amino acids are not stored in the body. The individual amino acids are broken down into pyruvate, acetyl CoA, or intermediates of the Krebs cycle, and used for energy or for lipogenesis reactions to be stored as fats.

card.q: Release of trypsin and chymotrypsin in their active form can result in the digestion of the pancreas or small intestine itself. What mechanism does the body employ to prevent its self-destruction?
card.a: Trypsin and chymotrypsin are released as inactive proenzymes. They are only activated in the small intestine, where they act upon ingested proteins in the food. This helps avoid unintended breakdown of the pancreas or small intestine.

q: During the absorptive state, glucose levels are ________, insulin levels are ________, and glucagon levels ________.
why: The correct answer is: high; high; are low. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Starvation sets in after 3 to 4 days without food. Which hormones change in response to low glucose levels?
why: The correct answer is: glucagon and insulin. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The postabsorptive state relies on stores of ________ in the ________.
why: The correct answer is: glycogen; liver. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “also called the fed state; the metabolic state occurring during the first few hours after ingesting food in which the body is digesting food and absorbing the nutrients”
why: absorptive state: also called the fed state; the metabolic state occurring during the first few hours after ingesting food in which the body is digesting food and absorbing the nutrients

q: Which term matches this definition? “form that glucose assumes when it is stored”
why: glycogen: form that glucose assumes when it is stored

q: Which term matches this definition? “hormone secreted by the pancreas that stimulates the uptake of glucose into the cells”
why: insulin: hormone secreted by the pancreas that stimulates the uptake of glucose into the cells

q: Which term matches this definition? “also called the fasting state; the metabolic state occurring after digestion when food is no longer the body’s source of energy and it must rely on stored glycogen”
why: postabsorptive state: also called the fasting state; the metabolic state occurring after digestion when food is no longer the body’s source of energy and it must rely on stored glycogen

card.q: In type II diabetes, insulin is produced but is nonfunctional. These patients are described as “starving in a sea of plenty,” because their blood glucose levels are high, but none of the glucose is transported into the cells. Describe how this leads to malnutrition.
card.a: Insulin stimulates the uptake of glucose into the cells. In diabetes, the insulin does not function properly; therefore, the blood glucose is unable to be transported across the cell membrane for processing. These patients are unable to process the glucose in their blood and therefore must rely on other sources of fuel. If the disease is not controlled properly, this inability to process the glucose can lead to starvation states even though the patient is eating.

card.q: Ketone bodies are used as an alternative source of fuel during starvation. Describe how ketones are synthesized.
card.a: When triglycerides and fatty acids are broken down, acetyl CoA is created. If excess acetyl CoA is generated in this process, the excess is used in ketogenesis or the creation of ketones. This creation results from the conversion of acetyl CoA by thiolase into acetoacetyl CoA. This acetoacetyl CoA is subsequently converted into β-hydroxybutyrate, the most common ketone in the body.

q: The body’s temperature is controlled by the ________. This temperature is always kept between ________.
why: The correct answer is: hypothalamus; 97.7–99.5 °F. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Fever increases the body temperature and can induce chills to help cool the temperature back down. What other mechanisms are in place to regulate the body temperature?
options: erection of the hairs on the arms and legs
why: The correct answer is: all of the above. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The heat you feel on your chair when you stand up was transferred from your skin via ________.
why: The correct answer is: conduction. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A crowded room warms up through the mechanism of ________.
why: The correct answer is: radiation. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “amount of energy expended by the body at rest”
why: basal metabolic rate (BMR): amount of energy expended by the body at rest

q: Which term matches this definition? “transfer of heat through physical contact”
why: conduction: transfer of heat through physical contact

q: Which term matches this definition? “transfer of heat between the skin and air or water”
why: convection: transfer of heat between the skin and air or water

q: Which term matches this definition? “transfer of heat that occurs when water changes from a liquid to a gas”
why: evaporation: transfer of heat that occurs when water changes from a liquid to a gas

q: Which term matches this definition? “amount of energy consumed minus the amount of energy expended by the body”
why: metabolic rate: amount of energy consumed minus the amount of energy expended by the body

q: Which term matches this definition? “transfer of heat via infrared waves”
why: radiation: transfer of heat via infrared waves

card.q: How does vasoconstriction help increase the core temperature of the body?
card.a: When blood flows to the outer layers of the skin or to the extremities, heat is lost to the environment by the mechanisms of conduction, convection, or radiation. This will cool the blood and the body. Vasoconstriction helps increase the core body temperature by preventing the flow of blood to the outer layer of the skin and outer parts of the extremities.

card.q: How can the ingestion of food increase the body temperature?
card.a: The ingestion of food stimulates digestion and processing of the carbohydrates, proteins, and fats. This breakdown of food triggers glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, fatty acid oxidation, lipogenesis, and amino acid oxidation to produce energy. Heat is a byproduct of those reactions.

q: A deficiency in vitamin A can result in ________.
why: The correct answer is: improper eye development or sight. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Rickets results in improper bone development in children that arises from the malabsorption of calcium and a deficiency in ________.
why: The correct answer is: vitamin D. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Consuming which type of food will help the most with weight loss?
why: The correct answer is: lean meats. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is stored in the body?
why: The correct answer is: phosphorous. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “relative amount of body weight compared to the overall height; a BMI ranging from 18–24.9 is considered normal weight, 25–29.9 is considered overweight, and greater than 30 is considered obese”
why: body mass index (BMI): relative amount of body weight compared to the overall height; a BMI ranging from 18–24.9 is considered normal weight, 25–29.9 is considered overweight, and greater than 30 is considered obese

q: Which term matches this definition? “amount of heat it takes to raise 1 kg (1000 g) of water by 1 °C”
why: calorie: amount of heat it takes to raise 1 kg (1000 g) of water by 1 °C

q: Which term matches this definition? “inorganic compounds required by the body to ensure proper function of the body”
why: minerals: inorganic compounds required by the body to ensure proper function of the body

q: Which term matches this definition? “organic compounds required by the body to perform biochemical reactions like metabolism and bone, cell, and tissue growth”
why: vitamins: organic compounds required by the body to perform biochemical reactions like metabolism and bone, cell, and tissue growth

card.q: Weight loss and weight gain are complex processes. What are some of the main factors that influence weight gain in people?
card.a: Factors that influence weight gain are food intake (both quantity and quality), environmental factors, height, exercise level, some drugs or disease states, and genes.

card.q: Some low-fat or non-fat foods contain a large amount of sugar to replace the fat content of the food. Discuss how this leads to increased fat in the body (and weight gain) even though the item is non-fat.
card.a: Although these foods technically do not have fat added, many times a significant amount of sugar is added to sweeten the food and make it taste better. These foods are non-fat; however, they can lead to significant fat storage or weight gain because the excess sugar is broken down into pyruvate, but overloads the Krebs cycle. When this happens, the sugar is converted into fat through lipogenesis and stored in adipose tissues.

q: Diabetes insipidus or diabetes mellitus would most likely be indicated by ________.
why: The correct answer is: polyuria. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The color of urine is determined mainly by ________.
options: byproducts of red blood cell breakdown
why: The correct answer is: byproducts of red blood cell breakdown. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Production of less than 50 mL/day of urine is called ________.
why: The correct answer is: anuria. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “absence of urine produced; production of 50 mL or less per day”
why: anuria: absence of urine produced; production of 50 mL or less per day

q: Which term matches this definition? “enzyme produced by leukocytes that can be detected in the urine and that serves as an indirect indicator of urinary tract infection”
why: leukocyte esterase: enzyme produced by leukocytes that can be detected in the urine and that serves as an indirect indicator of urinary tract infection

q: Which term matches this definition? “below normal urine production of 400–500 mL/day”
why: oliguria: below normal urine production of 400–500 mL/day

q: Which term matches this definition? “urine production in excess of 2.5 L/day; may be caused by diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, or excessive use of diuretics”
why: polyuria: urine production in excess of 2.5 L/day; may be caused by diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, or excessive use of diuretics

q: Which term matches this definition? “weight of a liquid compared to pure water, which has a specific gravity of 1.0; any solute added to water will increase its specific gravity”
why: specific gravity: weight of a liquid compared to pure water, which has a specific gravity of 1.0; any solute added to water will increase its specific gravity

q: Which term matches this definition? “analysis of urine to diagnose disease”
why: urinalysis: analysis of urine to diagnose disease

card.q: What is suggested by the presence of white blood cells found in the urine?
card.a: The presence of white blood cells found in the urine suggests urinary tract infection.

card.q: Both diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus produce large urine volumes, but how would other characteristics of the urine differ between the two diseases?
card.a: Diabetes mellitus would result in urine containing glucose, and diabetes insipidus would produce urine with very low osmolarity (low specific gravity, dilute).

q: Peristaltic contractions occur in the ________.
why: The correct answer is: ureters. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Somatic motor neurons must be ________ to relax the external urethral sphincter to allow urination.
why: The correct answer is: inhibited. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which part of the urinary system is not completely retroperitoneal?
why: The correct answer is: bladder. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “smooth or skeletal muscle surrounding the lumen of a vessel or hollow organ that can restrict flow when contracted”
why: anatomical sphincter: smooth or skeletal muscle surrounding the lumen of a vessel or hollow organ that can restrict flow when contracted

q: Which term matches this definition? “smooth muscle in the bladder wall; fibers run in all directions to reduce the size of the organ when emptying it of urine”
why: detrusor muscle: smooth muscle in the bladder wall; fibers run in all directions to reduce the size of the organ when emptying it of urine

q: Which term matches this definition? “skeletal muscle; must be relaxed consciously to void urine”
why: external urinary sphincter: skeletal muscle; must be relaxed consciously to void urine

q: Which term matches this definition? “smooth muscle at the juncture of the bladder and urethra; relaxes as the bladder fills to allow urine into the urethra”
why: internal urinary sphincter: smooth muscle at the juncture of the bladder and urethra; relaxes as the bladder fills to allow urine into the urethra

q: Which term matches this definition? “loss of ability to control micturition”
why: incontinence: loss of ability to control micturition

q: Which term matches this definition? “also called urination or voiding”
why: micturition: also called urination or voiding

card.q: Why are people with female reproductive systems more likely to contract bladder infections than people with male reproductive systems?
card.a: The longer urethra of males means bacteria must travel farther to the bladder to cause an infection.

card.q: Describe how forceful urination is accomplished.
card.a: Forceful urination is accomplished by contraction of abdominal muscles.

q: The renal pyramids are separated from each other by extensions of the renal cortex called ________.
why: The correct answer is: renal columns. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The primary structure found within the medulla is the ________.
why: The correct answer is: loop of Henle. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The right kidney is slightly lower because ________.
options: it is displaced by the liver
it is displace by the heart
it needs protection of the lower ribs
why: The correct answer is: it is displaced by the liver. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “cup-shaped sack lined by a simple squamous epithelium (parietal surface) and specialized cells called podocytes (visceral surface) that participate in the filtration process; receives the filtrate which then passes on to the PCTs”
why: Bowman’s capsule: cup-shaped sack lined by a simple squamous epithelium (parietal surface) and specialized cells called podocytes (visceral surface) that participate in the filtration process; receives the filtrate which then passes on to the PCTs

q: Which term matches this definition? “cup-like structures receiving urine from the collecting ducts where it passes on to the renal pelvis and ureter”
why: calyces: cup-like structures receiving urine from the collecting ducts where it passes on to the renal pelvis and ureter

q: Which term matches this definition? “nephrons with loops of Henle that do not extend into the renal medulla”
why: cortical nephrons: nephrons with loops of Henle that do not extend into the renal medulla

q: Which term matches this definition? “portions of the nephron distal to the loop of Henle that receive hyposmotic filtrate from the loop of Henle and empty into collecting ducts”
why: distal convoluted tubules: portions of the nephron distal to the loop of Henle that receive hyposmotic filtrate from the loop of Henle and empty into collecting ducts

q: Which term matches this definition? “arteriole carrying blood from the glomerulus to the capillary beds around the convoluted tubules and loop of Henle; portion of the portal system”
why: efferent arteriole: arteriole carrying blood from the glomerulus to the capillary beds around the convoluted tubules and loop of Henle; portion of the portal system

q: Which term matches this definition? “tuft of capillaries surrounded by Bowman’s capsule; filters the blood based on size”
why: glomerulus: tuft of capillaries surrounded by Bowman’s capsule; filters the blood based on size

card.q: What anatomical structures provide protection to the kidney?
card.a: Retroperitoneal anchoring, renal fat pads, and ribs provide protection to the kidney.

card.q: How does the renal portal system differ from the hypothalamo–hypophyseal and digestive portal systems?
card.a: The renal portal system has an artery between the first and second capillary bed. The others have a vein.

card.q: Name the structures found in the renal hilum.
card.a: The structures found in the renal hilum are arteries, veins, ureters, lymphatics, and nerves.

q: Blood filtrate is captured in the lumen of the ________.
why: The correct answer is: Bowman’s capsule. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What are the names of the capillaries following the efferent arteriole?
why: The correct answer is: peritubular and vasa recta. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The functional unit of the kidney is called ________.
why: The correct answer is: the nephron. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “enzyme produced by the lungs that catalyzes the reaction of inactive angiotensin I into active angiotensin II”
why: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE): enzyme produced by the lungs that catalyzes the reaction of inactive angiotensin I into active angiotensin II

q: Which term matches this definition? “protein produced by the enzymatic action of renin on angiotensinogen; inactive precursor of angiotensin II”
why: angiotensin I: protein produced by the enzymatic action of renin on angiotensinogen; inactive precursor of angiotensin II

q: Which term matches this definition? “protein produced by the enzymatic action of ACE on inactive angiotensin I; actively causes vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone release by the adrenal cortex”
why: angiotensin II: protein produced by the enzymatic action of ACE on inactive angiotensin I; actively causes vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone release by the adrenal cortex

q: Which term matches this definition? “inactive protein in the circulation produced by the liver; precursor of angiotensin I; must be modified by the enzymes renin and ACE to be activated”
why: angiotensinogen: inactive protein in the circulation produced by the liver; precursor of angiotensin I; must be modified by the enzymes renin and ACE to be activated

q: Which term matches this definition? “protein-forming water channels through the lipid bilayer of the cell; allows water to cross; activation in the collecting ducts is under the control of ADH”
why: aquaporin: protein-forming water channels through the lipid bilayer of the cell; allows water to cross; activation in the collecting ducts is under the control of ADH

q: Which term matches this definition? “formed by microvilli on the surface of certain cuboidal cells; in the kidney it is found in the PCT; increases surface area for absorption in the kidney”
why: brush border: formed by microvilli on the surface of certain cuboidal cells; in the kidney it is found in the PCT; increases surface area for absorption in the kidney

card.q: Which structures make up the renal corpuscle?
card.a: The structures that make up the renal corpuscle are the glomerulus, Bowman’s capsule, and PCT.

card.q: What are the major structures comprising the filtration membrane?
card.a: The major structures comprising the filtration membrane are fenestrations and podocyte fenestra, fused basement membrane, and filtration slits.

q: ________ pressure must be greater on the capillary side of the filtration membrane to achieve filtration.
why: The correct answer is: Hydrostatic. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Production of urine to modify plasma makeup is the result of ________.
why: The correct answer is: filtration, absorption, and secretion. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Systemic blood pressure must stay above 60 so that the proper amount of filtration occurs.
why: The correct answer is: false. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “rate of renal filtration”
why: glomerular filtration rate (GFR): rate of renal filtration

q: Which term matches this definition? “plant polysaccharide injected to determine GFR; is neither secreted nor absorbed by the kidney, so its appearance in the urine is directly proportional to its filtration rate”
why: inulin: plant polysaccharide injected to determine GFR; is neither secreted nor absorbed by the kidney, so its appearance in the urine is directly proportional to its filtration rate

q: Which term matches this definition? “pressure of fluid across the glomerulus; calculated by taking the hydrostatic pressure of the capillary and subtracting the colloid osmotic pressure of the blood and the hydrostatic pressure of Bowman’s capsule”
why: net filtration pressure (NFP): pressure of fluid across the glomerulus; calculated by taking the hydrostatic pressure of the capillary and subtracting the colloid osmotic pressure of the blood and the hydrostatic pressure of Bowman’s capsule

q: Which term matches this definition? “increased fluid retention in the interstitial spaces and cells of the body; can be seen as swelling over large areas of the body, particularly the lower extremities”
why: systemic edema: increased fluid retention in the interstitial spaces and cells of the body; can be seen as swelling over large areas of the body, particularly the lower extremities

card.q: Give the formula for net filtration pressure.
card.a: Net filtration pressure (NFP) = glomerular blood hydrostatic pressure (GBHP) – [capsular hydrostatic pressure (CHP) + blood colloid osmotic pressure (BCOP)]

card.q: Name at least five symptoms of kidney failure.
card.a: Symptoms of kidney failure are weakness, lethargy, shortness of breath, widespread edema, anemia, metabolic acidosis or alkalosis, heart arrhythmias, uremia, loss of appetite, fatigue, excessive urination, and oliguria.

q: Aquaporin channels are only found in the collecting duct.
why: The correct answer is: false. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Most absorption and secretion occurs in this part of the nephron.
why: The correct answer is: proximal convoluted tubule. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The fine tuning of water recovery or disposal occurs in ________.
why: The correct answer is: the collecting ducts. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “involves the descending and ascending loops of Henle directing forming urine in opposing directions to create a concentration gradient when combined with variable permeability and sodium pumping”
why: countercurrent multiplier system: involves the descending and ascending loops of Henle directing forming urine in opposing directions to create a concentration gradient when combined with variable permeability and sodium pumping

q: Which term matches this definition? “presence of glucose in the urine; caused by high blood glucose levels that exceed the ability of the kidneys to reabsorb the glucose; usually the result of untreated or poorly controlled diabetes mellitus”
why: glycosuria: presence of glucose in the urine; caused by high blood glucose levels that exceed the ability of the kidneys to reabsorb the glucose; usually the result of untreated or poorly controlled diabetes mellitus

q: Which term matches this definition? “specialized cell of the collecting ducts that secrete or absorb acid or bicarbonate; important in acid–base balance”
why: intercalated cell: specialized cell of the collecting ducts that secrete or absorb acid or bicarbonate; important in acid–base balance

q: Which term matches this definition? “tight junctions in which the sealing strands of proteins between the membranes of adjacent cells are fewer in number and incomplete; allows limited intercellular movement of solvent and solutes”
why: leaky tight junctions: tight junctions in which the sealing strands of proteins between the membranes of adjacent cells are fewer in number and incomplete; allows limited intercellular movement of solvent and solutes

q: Which term matches this definition? “found in collecting ducts and possess channels for the recovery or loss of sodium and potassium; under the control of aldosterone; also have aquaporin channels under ADH control to regulate recovery of water”
why: principal cell: found in collecting ducts and possess channels for the recovery or loss of sodium and potassium; under the control of aldosterone; also have aquaporin channels under ADH control to regulate recovery of water

card.q: Which vessels and what part of the nephron are involved in countercurrent multiplication?
card.a: The vasa recta and loop of Henle are involved in countercurrent multiplication.

card.q: Give the approximate osmolarity of fluid in the proximal convoluted tubule, deepest part of the loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, and the collecting ducts.
card.a: The approximate osmolarities are: CT = 300; deepest loop = 1200; DCT = 100; and collecting ducts = 100–1200.

q: Vasodilation of blood vessels to the kidneys is due to ________.
why: The correct answer is: less frequent action potentials. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: When blood pressure increases, blood vessels supplying the kidney will ________ to mount a steady rate of filtration.
why: The correct answer is: contract. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of these three paracrine chemicals cause vasodilation?
why: The correct answer is: nitric oxide. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “mechanism by which smooth muscle responds to stretch by contracting; an increase in blood pressure causes vasoconstriction and a decrease in blood pressure causes vasodilation so that blood flow downstream remains steady”
why: myogenic mechanism: mechanism by which smooth muscle responds to stretch by contracting; an increase in blood pressure causes vasoconstriction and a decrease in blood pressure causes vasodilation so that blood flow downstream remains steady

q: Which term matches this definition? “feedback mechanism involving the JGA; macula densa cells monitor Na⁺ concentration in the terminal portion of the ascending loop of Henle and act to cause vasoconstriction or vasodilation of afferent and efferent arterioles to alter GFR”
why: tubuloglomerular feedback: feedback mechanism involving the JGA; macula densa cells monitor Na⁺ concentration in the terminal portion of the ascending loop of Henle and act to cause vasoconstriction or vasodilation of afferent and efferent arterioles to alter GFR

card.q: Explain what happens to Na⁺ concentration in the nephron when GFR increases.
card.a: Sodium concentration in the filtrate increases when GFR increases; it will decrease when GFR decreases.

card.q: If you want the kidney to excrete more Na⁺ in the urine, what do you want the blood flow to do?
card.a: To excrete more Na⁺ in the urine, increase the flow rate.

q: What hormone directly opposes the actions of natriuretic hormones?
why: The correct answer is: aldosterone. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of these is a vasoconstrictor?
why: The correct answer is: angiotensin II. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What signal causes the heart to secrete atrial natriuretic hormone?
why: The correct answer is: increased blood pressure. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “group of vasoconstrictive, 21-amino acid peptides; produced by endothelial cells of the renal blood vessels, mesangial cells, and cells of the DCT”
why: endothelins: group of vasoconstrictive, 21-amino acid peptides; produced by endothelial cells of the renal blood vessels, mesangial cells, and cells of the DCT

card.q: What organs produce which hormones or enzymes in the renin–angiotensin system?
card.a: The liver produces angiotensinogen, the lungs produce ACE, and the kidneys produce renin.

card.q: PTH affects absorption and reabsorption of what?
card.a: PTH affects absorption and reabsorption of calcium.

q: Which of these beverages does not have a diuretic effect?
why: The correct answer is: milk. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Progesterone can bind to receptors for which hormone that, when released, activates water retention?
why: The correct answer is: aldosterone. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Renin is released in response to ________.
why: The correct answer is: decreased blood pressure. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “compound that increases urine output, leading to decreased water conservation”
why: diuretic: compound that increases urine output, leading to decreased water conservation

card.q: Why is ADH also called vasopressin?
card.a: When first discovered, it was named for its known activity—vasoconstriction.

card.q: How can glucose be a diuretic?
card.a: In cases of diabetes mellitus, there is more glucose present than the kidney can recover and the excess glucose is lost in the urine. It possesses osmotic character so that it attracts water to the forming urine.

q: Which step in vitamin D production does the kidney perform?
why: The correct answer is: converts calcidiol into calcitriol. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which hormone does the kidney produce that stimulates red blood cell production?
why: The correct answer is: EPO. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: If there were no aquaporin channels in the collecting duct, ________.
options: you would lose vitamins and electrolytes
why: The correct answer is: you would suffer severe dehydration. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “softening of bones due to a lack of mineralization with calcium and phosphate; most often due to lack of vitamin D; in children, osteomalacia is termed rickets; not to be confused with osteoporosis”
why: osteomalacia: softening of bones due to a lack of mineralization with calcium and phosphate; most often due to lack of vitamin D; in children, osteomalacia is termed rickets; not to be confused with osteoporosis

card.q: How does lack of protein in the blood cause edema?
card.a: Protein has osmotic properties. If there is not enough protein in the blood, water will be attracted to the interstitial space and the cell cytoplasm resulting in tissue edema.

card.q: Which three electrolytes are most closely regulated by the kidney?
card.a: The three electrolytes are most closely regulated by the kidney are calcium, sodium, and potassium.

q: Solute contributes to the movement of water between cells and the surrounding medium by ________.
why: The correct answer is: osmotic pressure. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A cation has a(n) ________ charge.
why: The correct answer is: positive. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Interstitial fluid (IF) is ________.
options: the fluid in the cytosol of the cells
the fluid that bathes all of the body’s cells except for blood cells
the intracellular fluids found between membranes
why: The correct answer is: the fluid that bathes all of the body’s cells except for blood cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “fluid exterior to cells; includes the interstitial fluid, blood plasma, and fluids found in other reservoirs in the body”
why: extracellular fluid (ECF): fluid exterior to cells; includes the interstitial fluid, blood plasma, and fluids found in other reservoirs in the body

q: Which term matches this definition? “fluid inside all cells of the body constitutes a compartment system that is largely segregated from other systems”
why: fluid compartment: fluid inside all cells of the body constitutes a compartment system that is largely segregated from other systems

q: Which term matches this definition? “pressure exerted by a fluid against a wall, caused by its own weight or pumping force”
why: hydrostatic pressure: pressure exerted by a fluid against a wall, caused by its own weight or pumping force

q: Which term matches this definition? “fluid in the small spaces between cells not contained within blood vessels”
why: interstitial fluid (IF): fluid in the small spaces between cells not contained within blood vessels

q: Which term matches this definition? “fluid in the cytosol of cells”
why: intracellular fluid (ICF): fluid in the cytosol of cells

card.q: Watch this video to learn more about body fluids, fluid compartments, and electrolytes. When blood volume decreases due to sweating, from what source is water taken in by the blood?
card.a: The interstitial fluid (IF).

card.q: Watch this video to see an explanation of the dynamics of fluid in the body’s compartments. What happens in tissues when capillary blood pressure is less than osmotic pressure?
card.a: Fluid enters the capillaries from interstitial spaces.

card.q: Plasma contains more sodium than chloride. How can this be if individual ions of sodium and chloride exactly balance each other out, and plasma is electrically neutral?
card.a: There are additional negatively charged molecules in plasma besides chloride. The additional sodium balances the total negative charges.

card.q: How is fluid moved from compartment to compartment?
card.a: Fluid is moved by a combination of osmotic and hydrostatic pressures. The osmotic pressure results from differences in solute concentrations across cell membranes. Hydrostatic pressure results from the pressure of blood as it enters a capillary system, forcing some fluid out of the vessel into the surrounding tissues.

q: The largest amount of water comes into the body via ________.
why: The correct answer is: liquids. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The largest amount of water leaves the body via ________.
why: The correct answer is: urine. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Insensible water loss is water lost via ________.
options: skin evaporation and in air from the lungs
why: The correct answer is: skin evaporation and in air from the lungs. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: How soon after drinking a large glass of water will a person start increasing their urine output?
why: The correct answer is: 30 minutes. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “also known as vasopressin, a hormone that increases the volume of water reabsorbed from the collecting tubules of the kidney”
why: antidiuretic hormone (ADH): also known as vasopressin, a hormone that increases the volume of water reabsorbed from the collecting tubules of the kidney

q: Which term matches this definition? “state of containing insufficient water in blood and other tissues”
why: dehydration: state of containing insufficient water in blood and other tissues

q: Which term matches this definition? “excess production of urine”
why: diuresis: excess production of urine

q: Which term matches this definition? “ratio of solutes to a volume of solvent in the plasma; plasma osmolality reflects a person’s state of hydration”
why: plasma osmolality: ratio of solutes to a volume of solvent in the plasma; plasma osmolality reflects a person’s state of hydration

card.q: Describe the effect of ADH on renal collecting tubules.
card.a: ADH constricts the arterioles in the peripheral circulation, limiting blood to the extremities and increasing the blood supply to the core of the body. ADH also causes the epithelial cells lining the renal collecting tubules to move water channel proteins called aquaporins from the sides of the cells to the apical surface. This greatly increases the passage of water from the renal filtrate through the wall of the collecting tubule as well as the reabsorption of water into the bloodstream.

card.q: Why is it important for the amount of water intake to equal the amount of water output?
card.a: Any imbalance of water entering or leaving the body will create an osmotic imbalance that will adversely affect cell and tissue function.

q: Bone serves as a mineral reserve for which two ions?
why: The correct answer is: calcium and phosphate. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Electrolytes are lost mostly through ________.
why: The correct answer is: renal function. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The major cation in extracellular fluid is ________.
why: The correct answer is: sodium. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The major cation in intracellular fluid is ________.
why: The correct answer is: potassium. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The major anion in extracellular fluid is ________.
why: The correct answer is: chloride. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Most of the body’s calcium is found in ________.
why: The correct answer is: bone. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Abnormally increased blood levels of sodium are termed ________.
why: The correct answer is: hypernatremia. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The ion with the lowest blood level is ________.
why: The correct answer is: potassium. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which two ions are most affected by aldosterone?
why: The correct answer is: sodium and potassium. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Read this article for an explanation of the effect of seawater on humans. What effect does drinking seawater have on the body?
card.a: Drinking seawater dehydrates the body as the body must pass sodium through the kidneys, and water follows.

card.q: Explain how the CO₂ generated by cells and exhaled in the lungs is carried as bicarbonate in the blood.
card.a: Very little of the carbon dioxide in the blood is carried dissolved in the plasma. It is transformed into carbonic acid and then into bicarbonate in order to mix in plasma for transportation to the lungs, where it reverts back to its gaseous form.

card.q: How can one have an imbalance in a substance, but not actually have elevated or deficient levels of that substance in the body?
card.a: Without having an absolute excess or deficiency of a substance, one can have too much or too little of that substance in a given compartment. Such a relative increase or decrease is due to a redistribution of water or the ion in the body’s compartments. This may be due to the loss of water in the blood, leading to a hemoconcentration or dilution of the ion in tissues due to edema.

q: Which of the following is the most important buffer inside red blood cells?
why: The correct answer is: hemoglobin. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which explanation best describes why plasma proteins can function as buffers?
options: Plasma proteins combine with bicarbonate to make a stronger buffer.
Plasma proteins are immune to damage from acids.
Proteins have both positive and negative charges on their surface.
why: The correct answer is: Proteins have both positive and negative charges on their surface.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The buffer that is adjusted to control acid-base balance is ________.
why: The correct answer is: bicarbonate: carbonic acid buffer. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Carbonic acid levels are controlled through the ________.
why: The correct answer is: respiratory system. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Bicarbonate ion concentrations in the blood are controlled through the ________.
why: The correct answer is: renal system. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which reaction is catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase?
why: The correct answer is: CO₂+ H₂O↔H₂CO₃. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Describe the conservation of bicarbonate ions in the renal system.
card.a: Bicarbonate ions are freely filtered through the glomerulus. They cannot pass freely into the renal tubular cells and must be converted into CO₂ in the filtrate, which can pass through the cell membrane. Sodium ions are reabsorbed at the membrane, and hydrogen ions are expelled into the filtrate. The hydrogen ions combine with bicarbonate, forming carbonic acid, which dissociates into CO₂ gas and water. The gas diffuses into the renal cells where carbonic anhydrase catalyzes its conversion back into a bicarbonate ion, which enters the blood.

card.q: Describe the control of blood carbonic acid levels through the respiratory system.
card.a: Carbonic acid blood levels are controlled through the respiratory system by the expulsion of CO₂ from the lungs. The formula for the production of bicarbonate ions is reversible if the concentration of CO₂ decreases. As this happens in the lungs, carbonic acid is converted into a gas, and the concentration of the acid decreases. The rate of respiration determines the amount of CO₂ exhaled. If the rate increases, less acid is in the blood; if the rate decreases, the blood can become more acidic.

q: Which of the following is a cause of metabolic acidosis?
why: The correct answer is: diarrhea. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is a cause of respiratory acidosis?
why: The correct answer is: emphysema. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: At a pH of 7.40, the carbonic acid ratio is ________.
why: The correct answer is: 20:1. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is characterized as metabolic alkalosis?
options: increased pH, decreased pCO₂, decreased HCO₃^–
increased pH, increased pCO₂, increased HCO₃^–
decreased pH, decreased pCO₂, decreased HCO₃^–
decreased pH, increased pCO₂, increased HCO₃^–
why: The correct answer is: increased pH, increased pCO₂, increased HCO₃^–. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “condition wherein a deficiency of bicarbonate causes the blood to be overly acidic”
why: metabolic acidosis: condition wherein a deficiency of bicarbonate causes the blood to be overly acidic

q: Which term matches this definition? “condition wherein an excess of bicarbonate causes the blood to be overly alkaline”
why: metabolic alkalosis: condition wherein an excess of bicarbonate causes the blood to be overly alkaline

q: Which term matches this definition? “condition wherein an excess of carbonic acid or CO₂ causes the blood to be overly acidic”
why: respiratory acidosis: condition wherein an excess of carbonic acid or CO₂ causes the blood to be overly acidic

q: Which term matches this definition? “condition wherein a deficiency of carbonic acid/CO₂ levels causes the blood to be overly alkaline”
why: respiratory alkalosis: condition wherein a deficiency of carbonic acid/CO₂ levels causes the blood to be overly alkaline

card.q: Watch this video to see a demonstration of the effect altitude has on blood pH. What effect does high altitude have on blood pH, and why?
card.a: Because oxygen is reduced, the respiratory rate increases to accommodate, and hyperventilation removes CO₂ faster than normal, resulting in alkalosis.

card.q: Case Study: Brooks is a 64-year-old admitted to the emergency room for asthma. Their laboratory results are as follows: pH 7.31, pCO₂higher than normal, and total HCO₃^– also higher than normal. Classify their acid-base balance as acidosis or alkalosis, and as metabolic or respiratory. Is there evidence of compensation? Propose the mechanism by which asthma contributed to the lab results seen.
card.a: Respiratory acidosis is present as evidenced by the decreased pH and increased pCO₂, with some compensation as shown by the increased total HCO₃^–. His asthma has compromised his respiratory functions, and excess CO₂ is being retained in his blood.

card.q: Case Study: Kim is a 38-year-old woman admitted to the hospital for bulimia. Her laboratory results are as follows: pH 7.48, pCO₂ in the normal range, and total HCO₃^– higher than normal. Classify her acid-base balance as acidosis or alkalosis, and as metabolic or respiratory. Is there evidence of compensation? Propose the mechanism by which bulimia contributed to the lab results seen.
card.a: Metabolic alkalosis is present as evidenced by the increased pH and increased HCO₃^–, without compensation as seen in the normal pCO₂. The bulimia has caused excessive loss of hydrochloric acid from the stomach and a loss of hydrogen ions from the body, resulting in an excess of bicarbonate ions in the blood.

q: What are male gametes called?
why: The correct answer is: sperm. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Leydig cells ________.
why: The correct answer is: secrete testosterone. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which hypothalamic hormone contributes to the regulation of the male reproductive system?
why: The correct answer is: gonadotropin-releasing hormone. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the function of the epididymis?
options: produces the bulk of seminal fluid
provides nitric oxide needed for erections
why: The correct answer is: sperm maturation and storage. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Spermatogenesis takes place in the ________.
why: The correct answer is: seminiferous tubules. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Watch this video to learn about vasectomy. As described in this video, a vasectomy is a procedure in which a small section of the ductus (vas) deferens is removed from the scrotum. This interrupts the path taken by sperm through the ductus deferens. If sperm do not exit through the vas, either because the person has had a vasectomy or has not ejaculated, in what region of the testis do they remain?
card.a: Sperm remain in the epididymis until they degenerate.

card.q: Watch this video to explore the structures of the male reproductive system and the path of sperm that starts in the testes and ends as the sperm leave the penis through the urethra. Where are sperm deposited after they leave the ejaculatory duct?
card.a: Sperm enter the prostate.

card.q: Briefly explain why mature gametes carry only one set of chromosomes.
card.a: A single gamete must combine with a gamete from an individual of the opposite sex to produce a fertilized egg, which has a complete set of chromosomes and is the first cell of a new individual.

card.q: What special features are evident in sperm cells but not in somatic cells, and how do these specializations function?
card.a: Unlike somatic cells, sperm are haploid. They also have very little cytoplasm. They have a head with a compact nucleus covered by an acrosome filled with enzymes, and a mid-piece filled with mitochondria that power their movement. They are motile because of their tail, a structure containing a flagellum, which is specialized for movement.

card.q: What do each of the three male accessory glands contribute to the semen?
card.a: The three accessory glands make the following contributions to semen: the seminal vesicle contributes about 60 percent of the semen volume, with fluid that contains large amounts of fructose to power the movement of sperm; the prostate gland contributes substances critical to sperm maturation; and the bulbourethral glands contribute a thick fluid that lubricates the ends of the urethra and the vagina and helps to clean urine residues from the urethra.

card.q: Describe how penile erection occurs.
card.a: During sexual arousal, nitric oxide (NO) is released from nerve endings near blood vessels within the corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum. The release of NO activates a signaling pathway that results in relaxation of the smooth muscles that surround the penile arteries, causing them to dilate. This dilation increases the amount of blood that can enter the penis, and induces the endothelial cells in the penile arterial walls to secrete NO, perpetuating the vasodilation. The rapid increase in blood volume fills the erectile chambers, and the increased pressure of the filled chambers compresses the thin-walled penile venules, preventing venous drainage of the penis. An erection is the result of this increased blood flow to the penis and reduced blood return from the penis.

card.q: While anabolic steroids (synthetic testosterone) bulk up muscles, they can also affect testosterone production in the testis. Using what you know about negative feedback, describe what would happen to testosterone production in the testis if a male takes large amounts of synthetic testosterone.
card.a: Testosterone production by the body would be reduced if a male were taking anabolic steroids. This is because the hypothalamus responds to rising testosterone levels by reducing its secretion of GnRH, which would in turn reduce the anterior pituitary’s release of LH, finally reducing the manufacture of testosterone in the testes.

q: What are the female gonads called?
why: The correct answer is: ovaries. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: When do the oogonia undergo mitosis?
options: at the beginning of each menstrual cycle
why: The correct answer is: before birth. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: From what structure does the corpus luteum originate?
why: The correct answer is: dominant follicle. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Where does fertilization of the egg by the sperm typically occur?
why: The correct answer is: uterine tube. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Why do estrogen levels fall after menopause?
options: There are no follicles left to produce estrogen.
The pituitary secretes a menopause-specific hormone.
The cells of the endometrium degenerate.
why: The correct answer is: There are no follicles left to produce estrogen.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The vulva includes the ________.
options: lactiferous duct, endometrium, and bulbourethral glands
mons pubis, labia majora, and Bartholin’s glands
why: The correct answer is: mons pubis, labia majora, and Bartholin’s glands. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Watch this video to observe ovulation and its initiation in response to the release of FSH and LH from the pituitary gland. What specialized structures help guide the oocyte from the ovary into the uterine tube?
card.a: The fimbriae sweep the oocyte into the uterine tube.

card.q: Watch this video to look at the movement of the oocyte through the ovary. The cilia in the uterine tube promote movement of the oocyte. What would likely occur if the cilia were paralyzed at the time of ovulation?
card.a: The oocyte may not enter the tube and may enter the pelvic cavity.

card.q: Follow the path of ejaculated sperm from the vagina to the oocyte. Include all structures of the female reproductive tract that the sperm must travel through to reach the egg.
card.a: The sperm must swim upward in the vagina, through the cervix, and then through the body of the uterus to one or the other of the two uterine tubes. Fertilization generally occurs in the uterine tube.

card.q: Identify some differences between meiosis in males and females.
card.a: Meiosis in the man results in four viable haploid sperm, whereas meiosis in the woman results in a secondary oocyte and, upon completion following fertilization by a sperm, one viable haploid ovum with abundant cytoplasm and up to three polar bodies with little cytoplasm that are destined to die.

card.q: Endometriosis is a disease characterized by the presence of endometrial-like tissue found outside the uterus—in the uterine tubes, on the ovaries, or even in the pelvic cavity. Offer a hypothesis as to why endometriosis increases a woman’s risk of infertility.
card.a: Endometrial tissue proliferating outside of the endometrium—for example, in the uterine tubes, on the ovaries, or within the pelvic cavity—could block the passage of sperm, ovulated oocytes, or a zygote, thus reducing fertility.

q: What controls whether an embryo will develop testes or ovaries?
why: The correct answer is: Y chromosome. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Without SRY expression, an embryo will develop ________.
options: male reproductive structures 50 percent of the time and female reproductive structures 50 percent of the time
why: The correct answer is: female reproductive structures. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The timing of puberty can be influenced by which of the following?
why: The correct answer is: all of the above. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “duct system present in the embryo that will eventually form the internal female reproductive structures”
why: Müllerian duct: duct system present in the embryo that will eventually form the internal female reproductive structures

q: Which term matches this definition? “life stage during which a male or female adolescent becomes anatomically and physiologically capable of reproduction”
why: puberty: life stage during which a male or female adolescent becomes anatomically and physiologically capable of reproduction

q: Which term matches this definition? “physical characteristics that are influenced by sex steroid hormones and have supporting roles in reproductive function”
why: secondary sex characteristics: physical characteristics that are influenced by sex steroid hormones and have supporting roles in reproductive function

q: Which term matches this definition? “duct system present in the embryo that will eventually form the internal male reproductive structures”
why: Wolffian duct: duct system present in the embryo that will eventually form the internal male reproductive structures

card.q: The different genitalia of fetuses develop from the same tissues in the embryo. View this animation that compares the development of structures of the female and male reproductive systems in a growing fetus. Where are the testes located for most of gestational time?
card.a: The testes are located in the abdomen.

card.q: Identify the changes in sensitivity that occur in the hypothalamus, pituitary, and gonads as a person approaches puberty. Explain how these changes lead to the increases of sex steroid hormone secretions that drive many pubertal changes.
card.a: As an individual approaches puberty, two changes in sensitivity occur. The first is a decrease of sensitivity in the hypothalamus and pituitary to negative feedback, meaning that it takes increasingly larger concentrations of sex steroid hormones to stop the production of LH and FSH. The second change in sensitivity is an increase in the sensitivity of the gonads to the FSH and LH signals, meaning that the gonads of adults are more responsive to gonadotropins than are the gonads of children. As a result of these two changes, the levels of LH and FSH slowly increase and lead to the enlargement and maturation of the gonads, which in turn leads to secretion of higher levels of sex hormones and the initiation of spermatogenesis and folliculogenesis.

card.q: Explain how the internal female and male reproductive structures develop from two different duct systems.
card.a: The internal reproductive structures form from one of two rudimentary duct systems in the embryo. Testosterone secretion stimulates growth of the male tract, the Wolffian duct. Secretions of sustentacular cells trigger a degradation of the female tract, the Müllerian duct. Without these stimuli, the Müllerian duct will develop and the Wolffian duct will degrade, resulting in a female embryo.

card.q: Explain what would occur during fetal development to an XY individual with a mutation causing a nonfunctional SRY gene.
card.a: If the SRY gene were not functional, the XY individual would be genetically a male, but would develop female reproductive structures.

q: Sperm and ova are similar in terms of ________.
why: The correct answer is: chromosome number. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Although the male ejaculate contains hundreds of millions of sperm, ________.
options: most do not reach the oocyte
most are destroyed by the alkaline environment of the uterus
it takes millions to penetrate the outer layers of the oocyte
why: The correct answer is: most do not reach the oocyte. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: As sperm first reach the oocyte, they will contact the ________.
why: The correct answer is: corona radiata. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Fusion of pronuclei occurs during ________.
why: The correct answer is: fertilization. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Sperm must first complete ________ to enable the fertilization of an oocyte.
why: The correct answer is: capacitation. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Darcy and Raul are having difficulty conceiving a child. Darcy ovulates every 28 days, and Raul’s sperm count is normal. If we could observe Raul’s sperm about an hour after ejaculation, however, we’d see that they appear to be moving only sluggishly. When Raul’s sperm eventually encounter Darcy’s oocyte, they appear to be incapable of generating an adequate acrosomal reaction. Which process has probably gone wrong?
card.a: The process of capacitation appears to be incomplete. Capacitation increases sperm motility and makes the sperm membrane more fragile. This enables it to release its digestive enzymes during the acrosomal reaction. When capacitation is inadequate, sperm cannot reach the oocyte membrane.

card.q: On Saturday night, a female has unprotected sex with a male. On Tuesday morning, she experiences the twinge of mid-cycle pain that she typically feels when she is ovulating. This makes her extremely anxious that she might soon learn she is pregnant. Is the concern valid? Why or why not?
card.a: Sherrise’s concern is valid. Sperm may be viable for up to 4 days; therefore, it is entirely possible that capacitated sperm are still residing in her uterine tubes and could fertilize the oocyte she has just ovulated.

q: Cleavage produces daughter cells called ________.
why: The correct answer is: blastomeres. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The conceptus, upon reaching the uterus, first ________.
why: The correct answer is: divides. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The inner cell mass of the blastocyst is destined to become the ________.
why: The correct answer is: embryo. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which primary germ layer gave rise to the cells that eventually became the central nervous system?
why: The correct answer is: ectoderm. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What would happen if the trophoblast did not secrete hCG upon implantation of the blastocyst?
options: The cells would not continue to divide.
The corpus luteum would continue to produce progesterone and estrogen.
Menses would flush the blastocyst out of the uterus.
The uterine mucosa would not envelop the blastocyst.
why: The correct answer is: Menses would flush the blastocyst out of the uterus.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: During what process does the amnion envelop the embryo?
why: The correct answer is: embryonic folding. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The placenta is formed from ________.
options: the mother’s endometrium and the embryo’s chorionic membrane
the mother’s endometrium and the embryo’s umbilical cord
why: The correct answer is: the mother’s endometrium and the embryo’s chorionic membrane. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: View this time-lapse movie of a conceptus starting at day 3. What is the first structure you see? At what point in the movie does the blastocoel first appear? What event occurs at the end of the movie?
card.a: The first structure shown is the morula. The blastocoel appears at approximately 20 seconds. The movie ends with the hatching of the conceptus.

card.q: Approximately 3 weeks after her last menstrual period, a sexually active woman experiences a brief episode of abdominopelvic cramping and minor bleeding. What might be the explanation?
card.a: The timing of this discomfort and bleeding suggests that it is probably caused by implantation of the blastocyst into the uterine wall.

card.q: The Food and Nutrition Board of the Institute of Medicine recommends that all people who might become pregnant consume at least 400 µg/day of folate from supplements or fortified foods. Why?
card.a: Folate, one of the B vitamins, is important for the healthy formation of the embryonic neural tube, which occurs in the first few weeks following conception—often before a woman even realizes she is pregnant. A folate-deficient environment increases the risk of a neural tube defect, such as spina bidifa, in the newborn.

q: The foramen ovale causes the fetal circulatory system to bypass the ________.
why: The correct answer is: lungs. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What happens to the urine excreted by the fetus when the kidneys begin to function?
options: The umbilical cord carries it to the placenta for removal.
It adds to the amniotic fluid.
why: The correct answer is: It adds to the amniotic fluid.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: During weeks 9–12 of fetal development, ________.

meconium begins to accumulate in the intestines

card.q: Visit this site for a summary of the stages of pregnancy, as experienced by the pregnant person, and view the stages of development of the fetus throughout gestation. At what point in fetal development can a regular heartbeat be detected?
card.a: A regular heartbeat can be detected at approximately 8 weeks.

card.q: What is the physiological benefit of incorporating shunts into the fetal circulatory system?
card.a: Circulatory shunts bypass the fetal lungs and liver, bestowing them with just enough oxygenated blood to fulfill their metabolic requirements. Because these organs are only semifunctional in the fetus, it is more efficient to bypass them and divert oxygen and nutrients to the organs that need it more.

card.q: Why would a premature infant require supplemental oxygen?
card.a: Premature lungs may not have adequate surfactant, a molecule that reduces surface tension in the lungs and assists proper lung expansion after birth. If the lungs do not expand properly, the newborn will develop hypoxia and require supplemental oxygen or other respiratory support.

q: Progesterone secreted by the placenta suppresses ________ to prevent maturation of ovarian follicles.
why: The correct answer is: FSH and LH. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is a possible culprit of “morning sickness”?
why: The correct answer is: decreased intestinal peristalsis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: How does the decrease in progesterone at the last weeks of pregnancy help to bring on labor?

card.q: Devin is 35 weeks pregnant with their first child when they begin experiencing diffuse, mild contractions for several hours. Examination reveals, however, that the plug of mucus blocking their cervix is intact and the cervix has not yet begun to dilate. Devin is advised to return home. Why?
card.a: Devin is very likely experiencing Braxton Hicks contractions, also known as false labor. These are mild contractions that do not promote cervical dilation and are not associated with impending birth. They will probably dissipate with rest.

card.q: Janine is 41 weeks pregnant with her first child when she arrives at the birthing unit reporting that she believes she has been in labor “for days” but that “it’s just not going anywhere.” During the clinical exam, she experiences a few mild contractions, each lasting about 15–20 seconds; however, her cervix is found to be only 2 cm dilated, and the amniotic sac is intact. Janine is admitted to the birthing unit and an IV infusion of pitocin is started. Why?
card.a: Janine is 41 weeks pregnant, and the mild contractions she has been experiencing “for days” have dilated her cervix to 2 cm. These facts suggest that she is in labor, but that the labor is not progressing appropriately. Pitocin is a pharmaceutical preparation of synthetic prostaglandins and oxytocin, which will increase the frequency and strength of her contractions and help her labor to progress to birth.

q: Which of these shunts exists between the right and left atria?
why: The correct answer is: foramen ovale. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Why is brown fat important?

It can be broken down to generate heat for thermoregulation.
It can be broken down for energy between feedings.
It can be converted to white fat.
why: The correct answer is: It can be broken down to generate heat for thermoregulation.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Describe how the newborn’s first breath alters the circulatory pattern.
card.a: The first breath inflates the lungs, which drops blood pressure throughout the pulmonary system, as well as in the right atrium and ventricle. In response to this pressure change, the flow of blood temporarily reverses direction through the foramen ovale, moving from the left to the right atrium, and blocking the shunt with two flaps of tissue. The increased oxygen concentration also constricts the ductus arteriosus, ensuring that these shunts no longer prevent blood from reaching the lungs to be oxygenated.

card.q: Newborns are at much higher risk for dehydration than adults. Why?
card.a: The newborn’s kidneys are immature and inefficient at concentrating urine. Therefore, newborns produce very dilute urine—in a sense, wasting fluid. This increases their risk for dehydration, and makes it critical that caregivers provide newborns with enough fluid, especially during bouts of vomiting or diarrhea.

card.q: Describe the transit of breast milk from lactocytes to nipple pores.
card.a: Milk is secreted by lactocytes into alveoli. Suckling stimulates the contraction of myoepithelial cells that squeeze milk into lactiferous ducts. It then collects in lactiferous sinuses and is secreted through the nipple pores.

card.q: A person who stopped breastfeeding suddenly is experiencing breast engorgement and leakage, just like they did in the first few weeks of breastfeeding. Why?
card.a: It takes time to establish a balance between milk supply and milk demand. When breastfeeding stops abruptly, it takes time for the supply to fall. Excessive milk supply creates breast engorgement and leakage.

q: Marfan syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Which of the following is true?
options: Female offspring are more likely to be carriers of the disease.
Male offspring are more likely to inherit the disease.
Male and female offspring have the same likelihood of inheriting the disease.
Female offspring are more likely to inherit the disease.
why: The correct answer is: Male and female offspring have the same likelihood of inheriting the disease.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: In addition to codominance, the ABO blood group antigens are also an example of ________.
why: The correct answer is: multiple alleles. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Zoe has cystic fibrosis. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?
options: Zoe probably inherited one faulty allele from her father, who is a carrier, and one normal allele from her mother.
Zoe probably inherited one faulty allele from her mother, who must also have cystic fibrosis, and one normal allele from her father.
Zoe must have inherited faulty alleles from both parents, both of whom must also have cystic fibrosis.
Zoe must have inherited faulty alleles from both parents, both of whom are carriers.
why: The correct answer is: Zoe must have inherited faulty alleles from both parents, both of whom are carriers.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Explain why it was essential that Mendel perform his crosses using a large sample size?
card.a: By using large sample sizes, Mendel minimized the effect of random variability resulting from chance. This allowed him to identify true ratios corresponding to dominant–recessive inheritance.

card.q: How can a female carrier of an X-linked recessive disorder have a female child who is affected?
card.a: The only way an affected daughter could be born is if the female carrier mated with a male who was affected. In this case, 50 percent of the daughters would be affected. Alternatively, but exceedingly unlikely, the daughter could become affected by a spontaneous mutation.
